argentine-constitution-1853:
Argentina adopted its constitution in 1853, after decades of civil war and the fall of the dictator Rosas. Delegates met at Paraná, since Buenos Aires had refused to join the new union. The thinker Juan Bautista Alberdi supplied the charter's blueprint in his book Bases, and the American constitution supplied its pattern.

The text builds a federal republic of provinces with a president, a congress of two houses, and an independent judiciary. A full bill of rights guards speech, property, worship, and movement, and the charter throws the country open to European immigration. Buenos Aires joined a few years later, and the charter, amended since, still rules Argentina today. It founded the modern Argentine state: the founding law of the nation's nationhood, built to end anarchy by law.
arxiv-2512-00053:
Nikhil Rout and Blaise Tine design a configurable dot product unit for GPU tensor computation. Efficient mixed-precision matrix operations are critical for deep learning workloads on general-purpose GPUs. Open-source designs often use separate arithmetic units, wasting throughput and silicon area.

Their unit fuses floating-point and integer pipelines into one architecture for inner dot products. It is built for the open-source, RISC-V based Vortex GPGPU's tensor core. A fused unit promises better utilization for mixed-precision AI on open hardware. A singular fused architecture replaces discrete arithmetic units, the design choice behind the throughput and utilization gains.
arxiv-2512-00153:
Networks fail, and planners need to know quickly how a failure changes what can flow through them. Mridul Ahi and co-authors design fault-tolerant data structures for maximum-flow and minimum-cut problems in a 2025 study. Their setting is unweighted directed graphs with a fixed source and sink.

Sensitivity oracles answer, after an edge change, how the best flow or smallest cut is affected, without recomputing everything. Fast answers matter for transport, communication, and supply networks that must react to breakdowns. The work is theoretical computer science, aimed at data structures that stay useful when graphs are damaged. Fault tolerance here means the data structure keeps answering after parts of the graph fail.
arxiv-2512-00553:
Reinforcement learning results are notoriously hard to reproduce: rerun the training and the policy changes. Bohan Zhang and co-authors study list replicable reinforcement learning in 2025, inside the probably approximately correct framework. An algorithm must return a near-optimal policy from a small fixed list, across different runs.

List replicability relaxes exact reproducibility to a shortlist: the answer may vary, but only among a few candidates. Formalizing that idea gives practitioners a target between impossible exact replication and anything-goes variance. Reliable learning algorithms are a precondition for deploying reinforcement learning in medicine, robotics, and infrastructure. A shortlist of policies is also easier for auditors to inspect after training. For teams who ship such tools, the gain is calm. A rerun may swap one good plan for a near twin, but it will not leap to a wild new one.
arxiv-2512-01253:
L Cheng and five coauthors study light-induced ferroelectricity in a crystal in a 2025 physics paper. Strontium titanate is a quantum paraelectric: it hovers near becoming ferroelectric, where a lasting electric polarization appears, without quite doing so. Intense terahertz pulses can push it over the edge briefly, breaking its inversion symmetry.

The mechanism behind that effect remains controversial. Using very strong fields, the team reveals second harmonic generation that varies across space in a patchy way. They attribute the pattern to competing lattice and defect dynamics. Sorting out the mechanism matters for fast control of materials with light.
arxiv-2512-01353:
Rongzhe Wei and co-authors show a new way to slip past AI safety guards. Guards block prompts that ask for harmful text. Most past attacks keep clear signs of harm in the prompt. Guards are now trained to spot those signs fast.

The new attack weaves harmful asks into harmless-looking prompts. It then uses a tree search that adapts as it goes. The aim is to hide the harmful sense from the guard. Work like this is shared so guard makers can test and patch the holes before real attackers find them.
arxiv-2512-01553:
Amy Li proves a vanishing result for Hurwitz spaces of marked covers. Hurwitz spaces collect ways one curve can cover another. Fully marked admissible covers add labels at key points. Their first cohomology group holds shape data about the space.

Li shows that group vanishes for covers of degree three. She then draws the same result for classic simply-branched covers. Vanishing results simplify the geometry of these spaces a lot. They help scholars count covers and study families of curves with fixed branching. Degree three is the first hard case, so a clean vanishing there hints the pattern may hold for higher degrees as well.
arxiv-2512-01953:
Long documents strain large language models because the key-value cache, their running memory of past tokens, grows in a straight line with text length. Sai Gokhale and four co-authors study in 2025 how to shrink that memory and the model itself, especially for deployment on small edge devices.

Single tricks are well explored: quantizing the cache, chunking the input, or quantizing the model's weights. What happens when they are combined, and which combination is best, was largely unknown. The authors examine these techniques jointly at the systems level, mapping the trade-offs. Their map helps engineers fit long-context models into tight memory budgets.
arxiv-2512-02053:
Sorting song lyrics by type or theme is a text classification job, and extra structural features can help if they are woven in well. Marco Gameiro's 2025 study builds the SFL Transformer, which feeds auxiliary structural features directly into the attention mechanism of a pre-trained BERT encoder.

Earlier designs fused such features only at the final output layer, after the text had already been processed. Gameiro's contextual gating instead modulates the hidden states inside the encoder stack, letting structure steer reading as it happens. The study also examines calibration, how well the model's confidence matches its accuracy, a trust issue for any classifier.
arxiv-2512-03353:
Six distances among four points reveal the shape of a space. Nina Lebedeva, Anton Petrunin, and Vladimir Zolotov study those relations in this 2025 work. They look at length spaces, where distance is the basic notion, and impose quadratic inequalities on the six distances in every quadruple of points.

Such conditions restrict how a space can bend and branch. The authors study what effects these quadratic comparisons have on the space as a whole. Results of this kind help classify metric spaces in geometry. They may also inform work on data sets viewed as abstract spaces. Quadruples are the smallest sets where such curvature signs first become visible.
arxiv-2512-03853:
Shuttling single electrons along a silicon chip is a promising way to link qubits, but real devices come with rough surfaces and stray charges. Jack J. Turner and colleagues simulate that transport in a 2025 quantum physics preprint. They focus on silicon metal-oxide-semiconductor devices, where conveyor-belt shuttling demonstrations lag behind a related material system.

Their full three-dimensional simulations solve the Poisson and time-dependent Schrödinger equations across shuttling speeds and gate voltages. At low gate voltages, extra screening from multi-layer gates collapses conveyor-belt motion into a bucket-brigade mode, exciting the electron's orbital state. Stronger confinement restores smooth transport, which proved robust against interface roughness, gate misalignment, and defects buried in the oxide. Defects sitting exactly at the silicon interface remain dangerous, though. Some can excite passing electrons or even capture them outright, marking the key challenge for reliable designs.
arxiv-2601-06753:
Yiran Rex Ma charts computational Chinese paleography in 2026 as a position paper. Chinese paleography studies ancient Chinese writing in its earliest forms. The field is undergoing a computational turn powered by AI.

He argues the field is evolving beyond automating isolated visual tasks. It moves toward integrated digital ecosystems for scholarly research, he writes. Reading bronze inscriptions and oracle bones involves many linked steps. Recognition, dating, and interpretation support each other in real scholarship. Digital ecosystems could join those steps into one research environment. His trajectory maps where the field has been and heads next. Digital humanities readers get a roadmap from a field remaking itself. The paper is a position statement, inviting debate and building.
arxiv-2601-07153:
Genta Indra Winata and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with can large language models understand, reason about, and generate Code-Switched text?. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Code-switching is a pervasive phenomenon in multilingual communication, yet the robustness of large language models (LLMs) in mixed-language settings remains insufficiently understood.

The authors present a comprehensive evaluation of LLM capabilities in understanding, reasoning over, and generating code-switched text. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07253:
Li Zheng and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to clean noise out of training data. The data trains Stable Diffusion, a tool that makes images from text. Foes can lace the data with noise that warps what the tool learns. The warped tool then makes poor images. Cleaning the data first is called adversarial purification.

Past cleaning tools were built for sort tasks, like naming what a photo shows. They miss tricks made just for Stable Diffusion. One such trick aims at the part that codes the image, the VAE encoder. A trick can also aim at the UNet, or at both at once. The authors set out a broad form of cleaning based on DDIM, a fast way to run the image tool. A new loss guides the clean-up, for data free of the foe's warp.
arxiv-2601-07353: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Tianyu Liu and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers talon. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Speculative decoding (SD) has become a standard technique for accelerating LLM inference without sacrificing output quality. Recent advances in speculative decoding have shifted from sequential chain-based drafting to tree-structured generation. Where the draft model constructs a tree of candidate tokens to explore multiple possible drafts in parallel. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07553:
Kabir Swain and colleagues introduce VirtualEnv, a simulation platform for embodied AI research, in 2026. VirtualEnv is built on Unreal Engine 5, a game engine known for realistic graphics. It evaluates large language models in interactive, task-oriented settings. Agents receive natural language instructions and must act in a virtual world. The platform also supports multi-agent tasks.

A figure in the paper lays out the full pipeline for multi-agent planning and execution. Users give instructions, and the system coordinates models that plan and carry them out. High-fidelity simulation lets scholars test agents safely and repeatably. Failures cost nothing, unlike tests with real robots. VirtualEnv aims to be shared ground for comparing embodied AI systems.
arxiv-2601-07653:
A large CHEX-MATE collaboration compares two ways of measuring the temperature of galaxy cluster gas. One way uses X-ray observations; the other uses millimetre observations. Both are often compared under simple assumptions: smooth gas with spherical symmetry. The authors note those assumptions create expected differences between the inferred profiles. Their 2026 preprint studies that relationship in CHEX-MATE clusters.

Galaxy clusters hold hot gas whose temperature profile traces the cluster's depth and history. If two methods disagree in a patterned way, the pattern itself teaches something. It can reveal structure in the gas or effects on cosmological estimates. The team works within the CHEX-MATE sample, built for such comparisons. Astrophysicists measuring cluster properties are the readers. The study helps them read method differences as information, not just error.
arxiv-2601-07853:
Zhi Yang and a large team benchmark the safety of AI agents that handle money. Financial agents powered by large language models now support investment analysis, risk assessment, and automated decisions. Their power to plan, call tools, and change mutable state creates new security risks. Finance is high-stakes and highly regulated, so failures are costly. Their 2026 preprint, FinVault, tests agents in execution-grounded environments.

Execution-grounded means agents act in a working system, not a chat simulation. Safety failures then show up as real bad actions, like wrong trades or leaked data. A benchmark built this way exposes risks that static question sets miss. Banks and fintech firms need such evidence before deploying agents. The paper serves AI safety and financial technology scholars. It supplies a testbed for agent safety where money moves.
arxiv-2601-08253: Marius Juston and three co-authors analyze how LDLT Lipschitz network layers behave at initialization. Their 2026 arXiv paper derives the exact output variance for these layers. The setup starts the parameter matrix with independent Gaussian entries of a stated variance. Lipschitz layers bound how much a network can amplify input changes, which aids robustness. Knowing output variance at the start guides scaling choices before training begins. The analysis helps builders set initial weights so signals neither vanish nor explode through deep stacks of such layers.
arxiv-2601-08453: Jakub Gismatullin and Patrick Tardivel link the beta distribution to associated Stirling numbers of the second kind. Their 2026 arXiv paper gives a formula for these numbers based on a moment computation. The moment comes from a sum of independent random variables with a beta distribution. From the formula, probabilistic methods yield lower and upper bounds for the numbers. Stirling numbers count set partitions, so new bounds serve combinatorics and probability alike. The bridge between a continuous distribution and counting numbers is the paper's neat turn.
arxiv-2601-08753:
Rishav Sen and four co-authors work on bus fleets that mix fuel types. Towns add more clean buses that run on stored power. A mixed fleet of clean and diesel buses is hard to run well. The price to charge a clean bus shifts through the day, so a poor plan can waste cash.

The team builds a plan that ties charge times to bus trips. It looks at grid price, bus routes, and charge point use at the same time. The aim is low cost with full service kept in place. A reader who runs a town bus fleet gets a way to cut charge bills. The plan also helps keep clean buses on the road more of the day.
arxiv-2601-09153:
Josue Martinez-Martinez, Olivia Brown, and Giselle Zeno test how to train image tools that hold up when shots go bad. Shots can blur, dim, or fill with rain and snow. A tool trained on clean shots may fail on the first storm. The team studies train plans that use a learned flaw maker. It makes true to life flaws, not just noise dots.

They add mix plans that pair wide flaw reach with sharp foe based fix steps. They also track if a tool knows when it is unsure, and how dear each plan is. A reader who ships sight tools gets a plan for storm proof train. It fits self drive and care scans, where a bad shot must not mean a bad call.
arxiv-2601-09253:
Zehua Liu and three co-authors use bad samples, not just good ones, to tune chat models. Plain tune uses dear expert text. A next path drafts many replies, keeps the best, and tunes on them. That path throws the rest away. Yet a bad reply holds sense: it shows what to shun, and how close a near miss can be.

Their method is called RIFT. A reward score grades all drafts, good and bad. Tune then uses each draft with a weight from its grade. No draft is waste. A reader who tunes models gets a data lean path. It may cut the need for expert text while it lifts the last score.
arxiv-2601-09353:
Ioannis Peridis and five co-authors plan car moves in a road with no lanes by a tree search led by a net. In a lane free road, cars can use the full width. That use can lift flow past lane roads. But each car must plan in a space with no lane rails to cut its picks. The search space is vast and shifts as all cars move at once.

They join Monte Carlo tree search, a look ahead by random tries, with a net that guides which tries to run. The net cuts the vast space to rich lines. A reader in self drive work gets a plan tool for a road form that may come, and that breaks lane based plans.
arxiv-2601-09653:
Balram Singh and five co-authors study a magnetic effect in wires bent through three dimensions. Their 2026 arXiv paper measures how geometry shapes exchange bias in tilted CoFe/IrMn microwires. Exchange bias arises where a ferromagnetic layer meets an antiferromagnetic one, pinning the magnet's preferred direction.

That pinning effect underlies many spintronic functions in use today. Moving it into 3D shapes lets researchers probe coupling on curved, non-planar structures. The tilt of the wire becomes a design variable. Results point toward spintronic parts that use shape itself, not just flat layer stacks, to set their behavior.
arxiv-2601-09953:
Christabel Acquaye, Yi Ting Huang, Marine Carpuat, and Rachel Rudinger ask if AI can judge how hard a math test item is. Test makers now pay for trial runs with real pupils. Those runs set the hard grade of each item. The team tests if open language models can do this grade work.

They find a split result. Models are poor judges when asked to rate an item at once. But when models act as fake pupils and try the item, the grades track real grades more well. The right setup is key. The work hints at a cheaper path to pre test new items.
arxiv-2601-10353:
Bowen Zheng, Minquan Cheng, Kai Wan, and Giuseppe Caire cut the packet cost of cache fed broadcast. A server with many antennas sends files to many users. Each user holds a cache of past files. Smart cache use can cut the load on the air.

Past plans oft split files into a vast count of parts. That split cost is named subpacketization. It can grow too fast to run. The team give a new build with a lean split. It uses a half sum pack of parts that do not clash. The aim is the same gain at a far lower split cost.
arxiv-2601-10453:
Victor Zheleznov, Stefan Bilbao, Alec Wright, and Simon King make modal sound synth that can learn. Modal synth builds sound from the tones of a thing. A string, a bar, or a plate each rings in such tones. Past modal tools are fixed once built. They can be slow to tune by ear.

High swings make the tones link in dense ways. The team give a form that stays firm as it runs. It can also be tuned by a learn step. Slopes flow through it, so a net can fit its terms to a target sound. The work joins old synth craft with new learn tools.
arxiv-2601-10553:
Jianhao Yuan and co authors fix the physics of AI made videos at run time. Top video tools make fine shots. Yet balls pass through walls and drops fall up. Such slips curb their use in real work. Past blame fell on weak physics sense from train.

The team say run time picks share the blame. They treat the fix as an align task at run time. A latent world model grades how true the physics is. That grade, named WMReward, steers the run. The aim is shots that look right and act right, with no fresh train.
arxiv-2601-10753:
Anik Chakraborty and Varinder Kumar build Fredholm theory on a twisted scale of Hilbert spaces. They start with the space of square-integrable functions on the unit interval. A unitary twist operator maps the standard Fourier basis to exponentials at half-integer frequencies. The weighted spaces that result form a scale, ranked by smoothness.

On this scale sits a diagonal operator with compact resolvent. Its spectrum is the set of half-integers. Frame theory, the study of redundant bases, supplies the approach. The work extends Fredholm theory, which governs when equations have solutions, to a setting built for half-integer modes. Such modes arise in problems with antiperiodic boundary rules.
arxiv-2601-10853:
Sandra Chulliparambil Shaju, Maria Azhar, and Karin Everschor-Sitte propose a new route to complex magnetic textures called hopfions. Three-dimensional topological spin textures draw interest for their rich geometry and possible device uses. A hopfion is a knotted swirl of magnetization, tied in a closed loop of twists. Making and keeping such knots is the hard part.

The authors introduce symmetry-transforming magnetic models. The idea is to generate and stabilize rich three-dimensional textures inside any magnetic background. If the method works broadly, hopfions could move from rare curiosities to design elements. They are candidates for dense, robust memory and computing devices that store data in knots of spin.
arxiv-2601-11053:
Qipan Wang, Tianxiang Zhu, Yibo Lin, Runsheng Wang, and Ru Huang present ATSim3.5D, a thermal simulator for 3.5D chip systems. The 3.5D style mixes stacked and side-by-side dies, which creates structures at many scales. Rising temperatures make thermal-aware design essential. Past tools struggle with both the multiscale structures and the nonlinear effects of high heat.

The simulator uses a nonlinear multigrid method, solving the heat problem at nested resolutions. Multigrid speed matters when designers iterate daily. Accurate heat maps for hybrid stacks guide floor plans before tape-out. The work extends the team's ATSim line to the newest packaging style, where heat paths cross dies, interposers, and packages at once.
arxiv-2601-11753:
Yicheng Shi, Jing Su, Anouar Rahmouni, and co-authors report work on quantum links. They send those links through fibre in the air at labs in the United States. Entanglement, a close quantum link, is a base step for quantum nets. Such nets could aid safe talk, sense work, and shared quantum computing.

Links that use light alignment are easy to make and to change. But fibre in use twists that alignment in ways that shift with time. The link must thus be held steady by active means. Their work deals with that steady hold over an aerial fibre line.
arxiv-2601-12053: Maël Donoso argues for a new base for AI: train foundation models on human brain data in a direct way. Today's models learn from text and other human-made data. That data is a filtered trace of a deeper brain process. Training on brain data could skip that filter. It could give models a more rich source of human thought. The claim is bold and raises hard points on data capture, scale, and ethics. The work sets out the case and the path it would need.
arxiv-2601-12153:
Arthur N. dos Santos and Bruno S. Masiero survey more than thirty years of automatic singing assessment and singing information processing. Both fields aim to aid singing teaching, performance study, and vocal training with computers.

One strand grades a singer by firm metrics, from live visual feedback to pitch tracking and spectral checks. The other matches a singer's voice to a target to read fine traits. The survey maps how both strands grew. Teachers and tool builders gain a full view of what works.  The survey spans work from the early days to now.
arxiv-2601-12453:
Amilcar Branquinho, Ana Foulquie-Moreno, and Manuel Manas study banded matrices of infinite size. A banded matrix has non zero entries only near its diagonal. Past theory gave spectral formulas for such matrices in the bounded case. The team push that theory past the bounded setting, into the unbounded case.

Their route uses shifts and factorizations of finite cut offs of the matrix. Each cut off, once shifted, splits into positive bidiagonal factors. That split is the key assumption of the work. From it, Favard type spectral formulas can be rebuilt for the full matrix. The results link to mixed type multiple orthogonality, a field with ties to random matrices and approximation.
arxiv-2601-12753:
Ruofan Li and Jiuzhou Zhao study a number theoretic property of prime ideals in number fields. Let K be a number field with ring of integers, and fix an element of that ring. For each prime ideal, they obtain a higher form of the alpha Wieferich property. Wieferich style conditions link exponent patterns to prime divisors in a rigid way.

Their result implies a nonexistence theorem for higher Wieferich unramified prime ideals. The title also ties the work to a conjecture of Erdos. Nonexistence theorems close doors that might otherwise waste search effort. They also sharpen what a conjecture must allow. The work sits in algebraic number theory, where prime ideals extend the role of prime numbers.
arxiv-2601-13253:
Ebubekir Tosun and co-authors give a mixed route to build large sense link sets for tongues with thin data. Their test case is Turkish. Sense links state how words relate, as kin, foes, or part to whole. Such sets feed search, teach tools, and language models.

Their route has three steps. First, fast word maps group words by sense with a cluster rule. Next, a large AI model tags the link in each group. Last, hand made dictionary sources are folded in to clean and grow the set. The mix aims for scale with care. Low resource tongue teams gain a plan they can copy with their own sources.
arxiv-2601-13853:
Kinga Słowik and Robert Wolak bring a classic map idea into the study of foliations in 2026. A foliation splits a space into layers, like pages in a book. For a Riemannian foliation, those layers carry a metric, a way to measure distance. The team defines a basic Albanese map for such spaces.

The map is built from basic 1-forms, which vary in a layer-friendly way. They relate this map to the classical Albanese map of the whole space. The study of its general traits is backed by key examples. New maps give geometers fresh tools to sort foliated spaces.
arxiv-2601-13953:
Gorgi Pavlov tackles a stubborn problem: teaching exact Boolean logic by gradient descent in 2026. Neural networks tend to settle on fuzzy approximations of logic. Those fuzzy forms degrade under quantization, when values are rounded to set steps. Precise logic needs sharp, exact choices at each step.

Pavlov's Hierarchical Spectral Composition selects spectral coefficients from a frozen Boolean Fourier basis. A Sinkhorn-constrained routing step composes them, with column-sign modulation. The design aims for logic that stays exact after training ends. Exact learned logic could serve chips, proofs, and safe control.
arxiv-2601-14353:
Özgür Sevinç, Özgür Ökcü, and Ekrem Aydiner link two ideas from gravity theory in this 2026 paper. One is MOND entropy, from modified Newtonian dynamics. The other is the extended uncertainty principle, which tweaks the basic quantum limit on what can be known at once. They build one unified framework from both.

The team starts from a higher-order version of the extended uncertainty principle. From it, they obtain a modified entropy-area relation. They then derive modified Friedmann equations, the rules for how the universe expands, by three distinct routes. The routes use the first law of thermodynamics, entropic gravity, and the emergence of cosmic space. They also check the generalised second law.
arxiv-2601-14453:
Christian Ferko, James Halverson, and Aaron Mutchler prove a broad claim about neural networks in this 2026 paper. They show that any quantum field theory admits a neural network description with a countable infinity of parameters. The claim extends to any probability distribution over tempered distributions. In short, field theory and neural networks can mirror each other.

As a worked example, they realize the two-dimensional Liouville theory as a neural network. They numerically compute the three-point function of vertex operators in that form. The result agrees with the DOZZ formula, the known exact answer. Readers get a proof of universality plus a numeric check that the mirror holds in practice.
arxiv-2601-14553:
Brian Christian and Matan Mazor study fair judgment in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM FAccT conference. Fair decisions require ignoring irrelevant, potentially biasing information. To do that, decision-makers need to approximate what decision they would have made had they not known certain facts. Examples are the gender or race of a job candidate.

That counterfactual self-simulation is notoriously hard for humans. It leads to biased judgments even by well-meaning actors. The authors test two aids: self-blinding and counterfactual self-simulation. Their title says these mitigate biases and sycophancy in large language models. Readers get methods for making both human-style and machine judgments fairer.
arxiv-2601-14653:
Yuyu Liu and five co-authors fill gaps in single-cell data in this 2026 paper. Missing data in single-cell sequencing datasets pose significant challenges for extracting meaningful biological insights. Existing imputation approaches often assume uniformity and data completeness. They struggle with cases where large patches of data are missing at once.

The team presents CROT, a Cluster-Regularized Optimal Transport method. It is an optimal transport-based imputation algorithm designed for patch-based missing data in tabular formats. Optimal transport fills gaps by matching distributions at the lowest cost. Cluster regularization keeps the filled values true to each cell group. The work is pure math. No new lab run is used, but the end terms feed straight into how the MUSE data will be read. Readers get an imputation tool built for the worst kind of missingness in single-cell studies.
arxiv-2601-14953:
Advaith Arun, Shiv Shankar, and co-authors work on how future wireless systems will gauge their channels. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with massive MIMO arrays, which use many transmit ports at once. More ports can raise spectral efficiency, the data sent per slice of spectrum.

The cost is overhead. Reference signals must be sent across the time-frequency grid, and they eat into data throughput. The team uses port cycling, a way to sound the channel with fewer ports at a time. Deep learning helps them estimate the precoder from that leaner data.
arxiv-2601-15353:
Asim H. Gazi, Yongyi Guo, and co-authors survey why reinforcement learning still struggles outside the lab. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with statistical reinforcement learning in the real world. The field has won in gaming, robotics, online ads, public health, and language tasks.

Yet a wide gap stands between research results and deployed systems. Two recurring challenges underlie much of that gap. The survey names the main obstacles to real use. It then sets out future directions that could one day close the distance between journal papers and daily real-world practice.
arxiv-2601-15553:
Quoc Anh Tran writes a note in non-abelian Hodge theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Earlier work by others built a map between two moduli spaces on a projective log smooth variety. One space collects logarithmic Higgs bundles with nilpotent residues. The other collects logarithmic connections with nilpotent residues. The known map between them is a continuous bijection.

Tran argues the map is in fact a homeomorphism, a stronger claim that also matches the spaces' topology. The note extends the picture to higher-dimensional quasiprojective varieties, per its title. Such correspondences link flat connections with Higgs fields across geometry.
arxiv-2601-16253:
Jay Farihi and coauthors report shifts in gas take up by a dead star with dust. Their 2026 preprint is a short letter on WD 0106-328. The star is a white dwarf with dust and rock waste in fall. Gas lines of two ions show the rate of fall. Six views span a full span of years with two big scopes, VLT and Keck.

The line strengths shift by a clear, firm count through time. Shifts mean the fall rate of waste is not fixed. A shift rate helps read how waste disks feed dead stars. It also tests if bursts of fall drive the change. The letter gives rare long term proof of such shifts.
arxiv-2601-16453:
Daniel Staros and three coauthors test how grain links bend the integer quantum Hall act. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Hall act in a square grid. In that act, flow steps sit at whole count marks. Links twixt grains can shift or blur those steps. The team varies link strength by a push term in the maths.

Runs show how steps move as the push term grows. Clear shift maps help read Hall tests in real stuff. Real stuff always holds some grain links in its grid. A map of link acts firms up the pure Hall tale. The work is a code run study of linked grids.
arxiv-2601-16653:
Jesús Algaba, Esteban Acuña, José Manuel Míguez, Bruno Mendiboure, Iván Zerón, and Felipe Blas study a form of ice that traps gas. Carbon dioxide hydrates form when cold and force squeeze gas and water. These solids matter for climate and for gas stores. How they first form rests on one key value. That value is the pull at the edge where hydrate meets water.

Just two past tests have gauged that edge pull, and both did so in a round-about way. The team's 2026 paper turns to screen models for a fresh gauge. Such models can track each small part of the mix. A sound value would sharpen forecasts of hydrate growth. It would also aid safe gas haul and storage plans.
arxiv-2601-16853:
Ian de Haan, Peter van der Putten, and Max van Duijn test how chatbots read minds in tales. Mind-read tests ask what a tale's folk think or know. Chatbots now score high on such tests. That sparks a row on what the scores mean. Their 2026 preprint asks if deep thought steps make scores more robust.

Thought-trained bots learn by steps with checked rewards. The team pits such bots on mind tests with twists. Twists can break bots that lean on stock cues. Robust scores would mean the bots track minds, not cues. The work helps labs judge social skill in bots with care.
arxiv-2601-16953:
Daniel Iľkovič and Jun Yan count lone point sets in a class of trees. A lone set holds points with no edge twixt them. Trees here branch in an r-way form with no flaws. A star set is all lone sets of a size through one point. Their 2026 preprint works out how those sets spread.

Counts by size and hub point fill the work. Such counts tie to hard sums in graph math. They also feed codes that place guards or hubs on nets. Pure counts on clean trees give base truth. Rough real nets can then be set next to that base.
arxiv-2601-17053:
Shuhao Que and a team of five co-authors keep gait tools true for old adults in rehab. Hip breaks need slow, tracked work to heal well. Wear tools can count steps and pace in that work. Most such tools were tuned on mid-age gaits. Old gaits are slower and less even, so tools slip. Their 2026 preprint uses fake data to pick sound traits.

Fake gait data fills gaps where real data is thin. Trait picks guided by fakes hold up on real old gaits. True counts help docs tune rehab with care. They also flag when a patient's pace slides back.
arxiv-2601-17253:
Yachan Liu and six co-authors ask which made-up zeolite-like materials could be made in real life. Zeolites are crystals full of tiny pores. Labs have made some of them. Computers have proposed vast numbers more. Most of those proposals may never form in fact. The team built ZeoNet-based classifiers to sort real from proposed forms.

They use three-dimensional neural networks on grids of distances inside each form. The abstract reports scores far above older tools. Gains are more than ten times those from shape filters or older learning methods. Such sorting helps labs spend time on forms that can work. It trims huge lists down to strong leads.
arxiv-2601-17353:
Houhao Wang and four co-authors built a catalog of phonon particles in real materials. Phonons are units of lattice vibration in a crystal. Some phonons carry chirality or topology, traits that shape heat and sound flow. Symmetry rules can predict such phonons. Yet no one had mapped the full set across material databases in a system-wide way.

The team set out to close that gap. They classify phonon emergent particles by symmetry. They also hunt for chiral phonons in known materials. A shared catalog helps labs pick materials for tests. It turns scattered case studies into a field map. Future work can start from known hosts, not blind search.
arxiv-2601-17753:
Roberto Crotti, Giovanni Denaro, Zhiqiang Du, and Ricardo Muñoz Martín tackle a gap in writing research. Their 2026 preprint presents Hylog, a tool for logging how people type. Most keyloggers miss the changes made by input method editors, the software that builds characters for scripts that are not based on an alphabet. That blind spot has limited studies of text work in such scripts.

Hylog joins two kinds of logging in one system. One side tracks each key press in fine detail. The other side tracks the text as it grows on screen. Put together, the two views give a fuller record of how a text is built. The tool is meant for researchers who study the mental steps of writing.
arxiv-2601-18253:
Peng Sun, Xiangyu Zhang, and Duan Wu build a scalable way to judge how happy users are with a chat assistant. Their 2026 preprint presents BoRP, short for bootstrapped regression probing. For open-ended assistants, classic A/B testing lacks reliable metrics. Explicit feedback is sparse, since few users bother to rate chats. Implicit metrics are ambiguous, since a long chat can mean delight or confusion. BoRP probes the model in a way that scales to many chats.

A high-fidelity satisfaction signal feeds the loop of product improvement. Without it, teams fly blind between releases. The method aims to give them a gauge they can trust at scale. Conversational AI lives or dies by such feedback.
arxiv-2601-18353:
Tuhin Chakrabarty and Paramveer Dhillon ask whether a machine can learn to write at the level of a skilled human author. For a long time, fine prose was seen as a craft that needs a human voice and a human sense of style. New text systems can now copy the voice of many authors in a few seconds, at almost no cost in work.

Their study tests what comes from training such a system on books of high worth. The claim in the title is that strong, expert level prose can grow out of that kind of training. The work speaks to a live debate for writers and teachers. It also matters for firms that sell text tools. If style can be learned from good books, the line between a human draft and a model draft gets much harder to draw.
arxiv-2601-18553:
Primož Kajdič and three colleagues report a new kind of edge on zones that ride in front of the Earth's bow wave in space. The Sun's wind hits that bow wave and piles up. Chunks of that pile can break off and ride on, with sharp rims of their own. Past work found two kinds of rim on such chunks.

The team found four chunks with a third kind of rim at one end. Two of them were caught by a fleet of craft that fly in a group. The rim is a known hot flow fault that forms when the wind meets a break in the field. A third rim kind shifts the tale of how these chunks form and fade. It also gives crews who watch space weather a new sign to track.
arxiv-2601-19153:
Zexu Pan and six co-authors pull a named sound out of two ear audio and say where it came from. Most sound extraction tools work on single channel audio and only isolate the sound. Real scenes are three dimensional, and two ear, or binaural, audio holds rich clues about where sounds sit.

Their system, LuSeeL, takes a language query, like a plain words request for one kind of sound. It then extracts that event and locates it in space. Hearing aids, robots, and smart glasses all need exactly this: pick one sound from a scene and know its direction.
arxiv-2601-19253:
Pascual Lucas and José Antonio Ortega-Yagües prove that two named surfaces are the only ones with a special line property. On a surface, isogonal lines cross the main curvature lines at matched angles. The pair ask which surfaces have all such lines be both generalized helices and pseudo-geodesic lines.

The answer is a clean pair: helix surfaces and the Enneper surface, and no others. A theorem that ends with a full list is a prized kind of result in surface theory. It closes the question and gives the two named surfaces a new mark of distinction.
arxiv-2601-20253:
Si Chen and five colleagues build a way to generate test benchmarks automatically from domain guidelines. Open-ended question answering tests whether a model can reason in context, not just recall facts. In practice-based fields, knowledge is procedural and rests on professional judgment, yet human exam sets for testing are often missing.

The authors use Bloom's taxonomy, a classic ladder of thinking skills, to shape the questions they generate from guidelines. A reliable generator would let hospitals, firms, and agencies test models on their own rules. That matters where buying or writing an exam by hand is too slow or costly.
arxiv-2601-20453:
The Tuan Hoang, Nhu Phong Tham, and Bao Quoc Tang study the fast reaction limit of a bulk-surface reaction-diffusion system. The system models a reversible chemical reaction with general stoichiometric coefficients. One chemical fills a bounded vessel, while the other lives only on the vessel's boundary, where the reaction takes place.

The authors investigate how the system behaves as the reaction becomes very fast, and at what rate solutions converge to the limiting one. Such limits simplify models of surface chemistry, from catalysis to cell membranes, where reactions at a wall drive everything inside.
arxiv-2601-20653:
Francois Baccelli, Diletta Olliaro, Marco Ajmone Marsan, and Andrea Marin develop a stochastic recurrence equation for multiserver jobs in cloud computing. Data centers face highly variable workloads: jobs may need one core or thousands, and run for milliseconds or for days. This variability limits how fully the infrastructure can be used.

The authors' equation models that queueing behavior for performance evaluation. Predicting delays and utilization under such spread is how operators decide capacity. A tractable model helps cloud providers promise service levels without wasteful overbuilding. With it, a team can test a new center on a screen long before it is built in steel and glass.
arxiv-2601-20753:
Zhiheng Jiang and five co-authors build a test bed for AI that must balance rival goals. Their 2026 paper presents GraphAllocBench, a benchmark for preference-conditioned policy learning. In this setup, one model must serve many users with different trade-offs. The model takes the user's stated preferences as input. It then produces a policy tuned to those weights.

The goal is to cover the Pareto front, the set of best compromises among goals. A single trained model should flex at run time, not need retraining for each taste. The benchmark tests how well policies land on or near that front. It gives researchers a shared yardstick for multi-objective reinforcement learning. Such tools matter wherever one system must serve people who value outcomes in unlike ways.
arxiv-2601-21053:
Thomas Cohen offers a teaching tour of a famous puzzle in quantum chromodynamics. His 2026 article introduces the Silver Blaze problem. The problem is a clash between two views of QCD with a chemical potential. At zero temperature, QCD stays in its ground state, the vacuum. All physical observables remain unchanged while the potential stays below a critical value. That stillness is the Silver Blaze property.

Naive reasoning suggests the system should respond sooner. Reconciling the two views takes care with how the theory is computed. Cohen writes pedagogically, for readers new to the puzzle. The article explains why the vacuum can stay silent under pressure. It is a guide to a subtle point in nuclear theory. Students of dense matter will find a clear entry here.
arxiv-2601-21153:
Liang Hong offers a new strategy to predict future insurance claims with honest guarantees. The 2026 paper treats prediction intervals in the regression setting. The field shows a paucity of finite-sample valid intervals for future claims. Finite-sample validity means the coverage promise holds at any sample size. It does not rest on large-sample math. Most old methods cannot promise that in regression.

Hong's strategy converts a method from one setting to another. It starts from a method built for the plain iid setting. It then turns that method into one for regression. The conversion keeps finite-sample validity. Insurers could quote claim ranges with certified coverage. Both regulators and actuaries value such honesty. The paper fills a noted gap in the field.
arxiv-2601-21253:
Wei Minn and six co-authors tackle a stubborn limit in automatic testing of Android apps. Good testing should visit as much of an app as it can. In practice, even the best current tools reach less than a third of an app's screens in real-world cases.

Their system, CovAgent, uses smart agents plus live changes to the running app. The agents plan what to try next, and the live tools let them get past screens that block simple scripts. The goal is to push coverage well past the old ceiling. Higher coverage means more bugs found before users ever see the app.
arxiv-2601-21353:
Qinhan Tan, Akash Gaonkar, Yu-Wei Fan, Aarti Gupta, and Sharad Malik adapt a classic chip-checking method for security. Formal checks can prove that a chip design keeps secrets from leaking to visible outputs. Both secrecy and integrity come down to whether information flows where it should not.

The underlying method, IC3, is a proven way to check safety properties. The authors tailor it to the flow questions that security checks ask. Off-the-shelf tools often struggle with those questions at real chip scale. A custom version could let designers prove security claims before any chip is built.
arxiv-2601-21553:
Keiya Sakabe, M. Levent Doğan, and Michael Walter settle a question about tensor complexity that has stood open since nineteen ninety-one. Strassen's asymptotic spectrum is a frame for measuring how hard tensors are to compute with. It feeds fields from computer science to quantum information.

A key issue is whether Strassen's support functionals are truly universal points of that spectrum. The authors show that they coincide with the quantum functionals, another candidate family. Settling the equality firms up the whole spectrum picture. It gives complexity theory a cleaner map of the landmarks it navigates by.
arxiv-2601-21653:
Vasileios Sevetlidis and George Pavlidis measure how a network's inner representation twists along a path through its inputs. Deep networks learn features whose geometry shapes both accuracy and robustness. Classic similarity scores compare sets of activations point by point, but they miss how features evolve along a path.

Two models can score as near twins yet react very differently to small nudges. Their gauge-invariant holonomy tracks the twist itself, in a way that does not depend on arbitrary coordinates. Path-aware geometry gives a sharper tool for comparing models and for spotting fragile ones before deployment.
arxiv-2601-21953:
Tathagata Banerjee, Maciej Olszewski, and Valla Fatemi examine the surfaces that limit superconducting devices. Resonators and qubits lose performance through dielectric losses in surface oxides. Labs fight those oxides with metal capping layers, surface passivation, and acid treatments.

The team studies how fabrication steps affect oxidation and contamination in bilayers of niobium with another metal. They use X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, which reads the chemistry of the topmost atomic layers. Their 2026 preprint connects processing choices to the surface states that follow. Quieter surfaces mean longer-lived qubits, so this kind of careful materials bookkeeping is part of how quantum hardware slowly gets better.
arxiv-2601-22053:
Sankha Subhra Bakshi and Gia-Wei Chern simulate what happens when interactions inside a material are suddenly switched. Such interaction quenches are a clean way to probe how strongly correlated electron systems behave far from equilibrium. The test bed here is the Hubbard model, a standard model of interacting electrons on a lattice.

Earlier theory, which treated the system as uniform in space, found coherent oscillations and long-lived transient states after a quench. The authors go beyond that uniform picture and report spatial textures that emerge after the quench. Their 2026 preprint shows the system does not respond evenly. Spatial structure in far-from-equilibrium states matters for experiments on cold atoms and quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-22253:
Katherine Muñoz-Mellado and four co-authors teach a neural net to sort quantum states by their links. Their 2026 preprint uses a type of autoencoder, a net that learns to copy its input through a tight code. The net learns to tell linked states from states that can split apart.

The team train it for pairs of parts, from the smallest size up to a much larger one. The net also learns to spot a second, softer kind of quantum link. It can tell bound links from free ones as well. Such fast sorting can help labs check states they make.
arxiv-2601-22353:
Vladislav Korostelev, Pjotrs Žguns, and Konstantin Klyukin study how hydrogen soaks into a class of oxides called brownmillerite perovskites. These crystals have a neat, layered atomic frame. Their 2026 preprint uses first-principles math to track what the soaked-in hydrogen does.

They work with two iron- and cobalt-based forms of the crystal. The hydrogen shifts the electron layout, the pull between magnetic atoms, and the favored spin paths. Such shifts could let makers tune a material with a gas, not a rebuild. The results give design rules for hydrogen-aware oxides. They suit sensors, cells, and switches.
arxiv-2601-22953:
Wavelet methods give a fresh handle on a classic quantum field theory in this study. The theory, named in the title, is studied in one space and one time dimension using a Hamiltonian approach that avoids small-step approximations. Daubechies wavelets in momentum space supply the building blocks.

Each wavelet carries a resolution and a position index, giving natural cutoffs at both fine and coarse scales. Those cutoffs make hard, nonperturbative problems computable. The setup could help study strong-force-like theories where standard expansion methods fail. Working in momentum space suits the analysis here, since wavelets there separate scales of motion in a natural way.
arxiv-2603-01453:
Some black holes at galaxy centers hide behind gas so thick that their X-rays barely escape. Xiaotong Guo, Qiusheng Gu, Guanwen Fang, and colleagues hunt for such hidden objects in the COSMOS field in this 2026 study. Theory says they should make up a large share of all active nuclei, yet surveys find far fewer.

The team picked more than a thousand active nuclei seen in infrared light but not seen alone in X-rays. Mid-infrared clues flagged a small set of strong candidates for the hidden class. Stacking faint X-ray signals backed that call, but the found share stayed well below what models predict. Host galaxies of found and missed cases looked alike, so the gap points to sources still too faint to catch.
arxiv-2603-01653:
Mateus Maia, Daniela Castro-Camilo, and Jethro Browell forecast weather-driven faults in power networks in this 2026 work. Storms and other harsh weather break lines and cut power, so early warning helps crews prepare. Forecasts must state their uncertainty clearly if managers are to place crews and stock with care.

Their frame gives odds for fault counts from hours ahead up to four days ahead. Common faults are modeled by blending several quantile fits, which estimate counts at set odds levels. Rare extreme bursts get a separate heavy-tail model built for counts. Weather ensemble forecasts feed the system, so weather doubt flows into fault doubt. Tests on two British networks beat standard practice, and a live trial with network engineers found the forecasts fit for real decisions.
arxiv-2603-01953:
Pengyuan Wu, Pingrui Zhang, Zhigang Wang, and colleagues add real-time correction to diffusion-based robot policies. Their 2026 work tackles a weakness: diffusion policies excel at manipulation, yet they react slowly when scenes change mid-task. Delayed responses in dynamic settings can turn into outright task failures.

Their framework, DCDP, pairs chunk-based action generation with live correction and needs no retraining. A self-supervised encoder reads dynamic features, and cross-attention fuses them into the policy. An asymmetric action encoder-decoder injects scene dynamics before each action chunk executes. In dynamic pushing simulations, adaptability rises by a clear margin at tiny extra compute cost. The modular design plugs into existing policies, and tests extend to real-world manipulation tasks with moving conditions.
arxiv-2603-02453:
Tamal RoyChowdhury, V Gayathri, Rossella Gamba, and colleagues measure bias from ignoring oval orbits in black hole mergers in this 2026 paper. Black holes formed in dense groups may keep oval orbits when detectors hear them. Most analyses still assume near-circular orbits, for speed and simplicity. That shortcut could skew the traits inferred from each merger.

The team injects eccentric signals from a high-grade model into the analysis pipeline. A standard circular model then tries to recover their traits. Small eccentric values stay safe, but moderate ones bias mass, spin, tilt, and distance. Circular templates fake the oval effect by inventing extra wobble, a deep confusion. Heavy, mid-eccentric mergers suffer worst. The results map where eccentric models become a must.
arxiv-2603-02653:
Minseo Jeon, Junwoo Jung, Daewon Gwak, and colleagues question three habits of recommender systems in their 2026 paper AlphaFree. Most systems store a learned vector for each user, start from raw item IDs, and use graph neural networks. Those habits cost memory and struggle with new users or items.

AlphaFree drops all three habits at once. It infers tastes on the fly, swaps raw IDs for language-based item descriptions, and learns from similar items without a graph network. In tests on real-world data it beat rival methods, with gains up to about forty percent over some baselines. It also cut graphics memory use by up to sixty-nine percent.
arxiv-2603-03053:
A. Lacquement, H. Beust, G. Duchêne, and A.-M. Lagrange ask whether a hidden planet sculpts the disk around the young star TWA 7. Space telescope images recently revealed a directly seen outer planet at wide separation. The debris disk also shows a sharp inner edge and a lopsided, horseshoe-like spread of material.

Combining N-body simulations with long-term perturbation theory, they test an unseen inner companion. A planet smaller than Jupiter, orbiting inside the disk edge, reproduces the sharp cutoff. Long-term tugs between the planets further demand nearly circular orbits, or the outer planet's companion material would be destabilized. The whole system looks dynamically cold, with planets and disk sharing calm, aligned orbits.

Charlotte Brontë published Villette in 1853, her most psychologically intricate novel of inner life. The book is a landmark of interior narrative and unconsummated desire in Victorian fiction and beyond. It draws on her own years as a teacher in Brussels, thinly masked as Villette.

Auguste Comte's main work reached English readers in 1853, in Harriet Martineau's short version. Comte, a French thinker, held that sound knowledge rests on facts we can observe. dickens-bleak-house-1853:

A crossing sweeper, Jo, spreads disease and shows how all ranks link in London. The suit ends when costs eat the whole estate it fought over for years.
