dumas-countess-of-charny-1853:
Alexandre Dumas published The Countess of Charny in 1853, climax of his Marie Antoinette romances in French. Henry Llewellyn Williams made this English version of the Revolution's climax and Louis XVI's end. The vast serial brought Dumas's revolutionary cycle to its scaffold close in Paris at last.

Andrée, now Countess of Charny, and Gilbert move through the monarchy's fall and the Terror's rise. The royal family's flight to Varennes, the Temple prison, and the king's trial fill these pages. Old friends from the earlier romances meet fates of exile, madness, and the guillotine in Paris. Dumas pauses for long views of the crowd, the court, and the Revolution's driving ideas in France. The cycle ends in elegy for a world the Revolution swept wholly away.
europmc-pmc10009953:
Lawrence and colleagues review the roles of reactive astrocytes in brain disease in a 2023 systematic review. Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells in the brain. After injury or during inflammation, signals from other brain cells can push them into a toxic state that harms nearby nerve cells.

The review pulls together studies on this harmful form and on milder reactive forms. It asks when these cells protect the brain and when they drive damage. The paper gives a balanced guide to a debate that shapes research on stroke, infection, and memory loss.
europmc-pmc10253853:
González and co-authors give a critical overview of the links between high blood sugar and oxidative stress in a 2023 review. The body burns glucose using oxygen, mostly in mitochondria, the cell's powerhouses. When sugar stays high, as in diabetes, harmful oxygen byproducts build up and damage tissue, and that damage in turn worsens sugar control.

The review traces this two-way relationship in detail. It covers the main chemical routes and the organs most harmed. It also weighs treatments that target the stress. The paper ties two core problems of diabetes into one account.
europmc-pmc1074353:
Moriyama and co-authors showed in 2005 how swelling chemicals sharpen a pain sensor in mice. The chemicals are prostaglandins, made at sites of injury. Two of them, PGE2 and PGI2, are known pain drivers. Their partner receptors in that role were still in doubt.

The sensor is TRPV1, a channel on pain nerve cells that fires with heat and spice. In lab cells and mouse nerve cells, the two chemicals boosted TRPV1 through receptors EP1 and IP. Moriyama found the boost cut the heat trigger to below 35 degrees Celsius. Body heat alone could then fire the channel. Mice that lacked TRPV1 or EP1 felt far less heat pain from the chemicals.
europmc-pmc10773453:
Revell presented phytools 2.0 in 2024, an updated R software pack for family tree studies in biology. Such studies use a species tree to infer how traits evolve, how fast groups split, and where they lived. The pack has grown over ten years into a core tool for that work. It now holds hundreds of functions.

Version 2.0 adds fresh tools and updates old ones, Revell reports. Tasks span fitting trait change models and rebuilding the states of ancestors. Users can also study how fast lineages branch and draw trees with data laid on top. Sample workflows walk through the most used paths in the pack. The pack stays free for any R user.
europmc-pmc1182353:
Bendtsen and co-authors built a 2005 computer tool called TatP. The tool hunts for a special tag on bacterial proteins. Proteins with that tag leave the cell by their own export route. That route differs from the standard export path most proteins use.

TatP learned from known tagged proteins how to spot the signal. It correctly found most known cases in tests. It also made far fewer false alarms than simple pattern searches. Bendtsen made the tool public so labs can screen genomes. Better tag calls help map how bacteria ship proteins.
europmc-pmc1241553:
Flake, Andersen, and Dixon reviewed uterine fibroids, benign womb tumors, in 2003. Fibroids develop in most American women over a lifetime. About one third develop symptoms from them. They are the top reason for hysterectomy in the United States.

Risk runs higher with age, African-American ancestry, no prior births, and obesity. About 40 percent of tumors show nonrandom chromosome changes. Estrogen and progesterone promote fibroid growth. Growth factors found at high levels in fibroids may carry out that promotion. Flake sums up what triggers remain unknown and what clues exist. The role of hormone-like chemicals from the environment was only just being explored at the time.
europmc-pmc1253653:
Gee and Payne-Sturges built a framework for racial health gaps tied to environment in 2004. Social and environmental factors clearly interact to produce disparities. How they interact stayed vague in past work. The environmental justice movement pointed to higher hazard exposure in poor areas.

Stress from social conditions is their proposed linking factor. Chronic stress alters immune and other body systems. It can also lead straight to illness. Residential segregation shapes who faces community stress and hazards together. Gee merges exposure science with stress biology into one model. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2004. It ran in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2004.
europmc-pmc1475653:
A rare syndrome makes the body attack its own hormone glands. Meager and co-authors studied patients with autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 in 2006. The cause is a faulty gene, AIRE, that teaches the immune system to spare the self. The team tested blood for antibodies that block interferons, proteins that fight viruses.

Every one of 76 patients from Finland and Norway carried strong blocking antibodies to most type I interferons. The antibodies showed up early, even before the yeast infections that often come first. Levels topped those in patients with a related tumor condition. Meager suggests these antibodies could serve as an early marker of the syndrome.
europmc-pmc1654153:
Grape berries resist clean RNA extraction, yet gene studies of ripening depend on it. Reid and co-authors fixed the method in 2006, adjusting for the berries' low pH and high sugar and phenol loads. The tweak improved RNA precipitation from berry skin and seed.

They then validated yardstick genes for Cabernet Sauvignon berry skin, testing 14 candidates with three statistical approaches. Several proved fairly stable, but no single gene won under all three methods. Using several yardsticks together beat using one. Reid also showed the payoff by tracking two genes, for water and sugar transport, across berry development.
europmc-pmc1810553:
Harrow and colleagues described GENCODE in 2006, the reference gene annotation for the ENCODE project regions. Those regions cover one percent of the human genome, chosen for detailed study. GENCODE aimed to find and map every protein-coding gene inside them.

The work combined hand annotation by the HAVANA team with lab validation and then refinement. Gene features fell into eight classes, of which only two count as confidently protein-coding. Of 420 coding loci tested by lab methods, 229 products were sequenced. They supported lengthened gene starts at 30 loci and new splice variants at 50 loci. A further 46 loci without coding evidence were validated as transcripts. The final set held 487 loci, of which 434 were coding.
europmc-pmc1876453:
Proffit, Turvey and Phillips updated in 2007 the stability ranking for jaw surgery that repositions the face bones. Orthognathic surgery moves the jaws to fix bite and facial balance, and metal rigid fixation holds the bones while they heal. Not all movements stay put equally well, so surgeons plan around a known hierarchy.

Two additions join the list: fixing facial asymmetry holds well with rigid fixation, and chin repositioning is very stable. In the first year after surgery, corrections for Class II long-face patterns held better than those for Class III patterns. Between one and five years the picture flips, with Class III patients then more stable. Changes over two millimeters occurred in a surprisingly large share of patients even after healing. Teeth usually adapt, so bite changes lag behind bone changes.
europmc-pmc2008453:
Cole, Jones and Todd reported an early trial in 1971 of a new anti-oestrogen drug, ICI46474, for advanced breast cancer. Anti-oestrogens block oestrogen, a hormone that can fuel some breast cancers. Hormone treatment was standard for late or returning cancer, but only some patients responded. The team treated 46 patients whose cancer was advanced or had come back.

Ten patients showed a good response to the drug. That rate matched what doctors saw with oestrogens and androgens, the older hormone options. The clear advantage was tolerability, meaning how easily patients could bear it. Troublesome side effects were uncommon. The authors present the drug as a useful new option for palliation, care aimed at easing disease rather than curing it.
europmc-pmc2125253: A medical paper with a method for cultivating Treponema pallidum in fluid media. The syphilis germ, grown. This article preserves that bacteriology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128353: A medical paper on antagonistic growth-activating and growth-inhibiting principles in serum. The serum's push-pull. This article preserves that cell biology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131153: Rabbits built their defenses over days, and this paper followed agglutinins and protective antibodies as they rose. Blood samples charted the immune climb. The growing protection, tracked. The article preserves that immunology research. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140653: How fast trypsin digests depends on the conditions around it, which this kinetics paper worked out in detail. The team varied the reaction setup and clocked the enzyme. The protein-cutter's pace, established. The article preserves that biochemistry research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2222953:
Gabriel, Herwig and Klenk showed in 2008 how influenza A adapts to new hosts through its copying machinery. An avian virus strain became mouse-adapted through mutations in its polymerase proteins and nucleocapsid protein. Those changes raised transcription and replication in mammalian cells. The team focused on two mutations, N319K in NP and D701N in PB2, and asked how they help the proteins enter the cell nucleus.

Both mutations strengthened binding to importin alpha1, the mammalian shuttle that carries cargo into the nucleus. Binding was followed by faster nuclear transport of PB2 and NP in mammalian cells. Importin temporarily gathered in the nucleus and drained from the cytoplasm. No such enhancement occurred in avian cells. Adapting to the host's nuclear import machinery is thus a key step in cross-species transmission.
europmc-pmc2329653:
Oren surveyed salt-loving microbes in this 2008 review. Such microbes are called halophiles, meaning salt lovers, and they live in places like salt lakes and salt pans. They appear in all three domains of life, the broad groups named Bacteria, Archaea, and eukaryotes.

Oren described two main ways these cells balance salt. Some fill their insides with potassium chloride, which forces all their proteins to work in near-saturated salt. Their proteins are highly acidic and fall apart in fresh water. Others keep salt out and make harmless organic solutes instead, such as ectoine and glycine betaine. That second group copes with a much wider range of salt levels. One red bacterium, Salinibacter, uses the salt-in plan and shares many genes with salt-loving Archaea.
europmc-pmc2361453:
Cassidy and co-authors built the LLP risk model for lung cancer in 2008. The model estimates a person's chance of developing lung cancer within five years from their risk factors. Such estimates could pick who should get early screening, since lung cancer found late is rarely curable.

They built the model from 579 lung cancer patients and 1,157 matched controls in Liverpool. Smoking, family history, asbestos exposure, and other factors went into the final version. For example, a 77-year-old male non-smoker with early family cases and asbestos exposure scored a risk of 3.17% over five years. Testing showed the model separated future cases from non-cases fairly well, with an accuracy measure of 0.70 on a scale where 1 is perfect. The authors said outside checks should come before clinical use.
europmc-pmc2361853:
Burnet and colleagues argued in 2005 that cancer research money should be judged against years of life lost, not just deaths. Years of life lost adds up how many years each death cuts short. A cancer killing young people scores far higher than one killing mostly the very old.

They compared 17 cancer sites in Britain, where the national research budget was about 250 million pounds. On this measure, cancers of the ovary, cervix, and brain looked much bigger burdens than raw death counts suggest. Brain tumor patients lost the most life each, just over 20 years on average, while prostate cancer lost the least, at 6.1 years per death. Lung cancer stayed underfunded on both measures. Brain, cervix, kidney cancers and melanoma stood out as high-burden but low-spending sites.
europmc-pmc2395253:
Henegar and a large team profiled fat tissue from obese people in 2008. Obesity research often focuses on fat cells themselves, but the tissue around them, the extracellular matrix, also changes. This matrix is the scaffold of proteins that holds cells in place.

Comparing white fat from obese and lean subjects, they found a clear gene activity signature in obesity. The obese tissue showed more interstitial fibrosis, meaning extra scar-like scaffold laid down between cells. It also held more infiltrating inflammatory cells, immune cells drawn into the tissue. The authors argued the stiffened matrix is not a side detail but part of the disease process in human obesity. A tight scaffold can squeeze fat cells and fuel the inflammation that drives obesity's complications.
europmc-pmc2569153:
de Vries, Ramrattan, Smorenburg, Gouma, and Boermeester systematically reviewed in 2008 how often hospital patients are harmed by their care. Adverse events, unintended injuries caused by treatment rather than disease, were recognised as a grave problem, but no pooled picture existed. The authors searched the major medical databases and selected studies that reviewed patient records for such events.

Eight studies covering 74,485 records qualified. The median rate of in-hospital adverse events came to 9.2 percent, so nearly one patient in ten was affected, and a median of 43.5 percent of events were judged preventable. Most patients suffered no or minor disability, but 7.4 percent of events were lethal. Operations accounted for 39.6 percent of events and medications for 15.1 percent, marking where prevention efforts should concentrate.
europmc-pmc2648953:
Lyons and colleagues described in 2009 a Welsh databank that links health and social care records for research while hiding who people are. Services collect huge amounts of data on patients every day. Joining those records up could improve care and science, but privacy rules demand strong safeguards.

Their system, called SAIL, had already loaded over 500 million records from many providers. The team built a matching program that gives each person a coded tag, so records join without names attached. They tested how well the national health number works as the matching key. The method proved right more than 99 times in 100 at spotting true matches, while missed matches stayed low. Care records, hospital records, and social service files were then tied to one register with the same approach.
europmc-pmc2654153:
Merabishvili and co-authors described in 2009 how they made a small batch of bacteria-killing viruses, called bacteriophages, pure enough to test in burn patients. Phages infect and burst specific bacteria. The mix aimed at two germs that often infect burns, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, in a Brussels military hospital.

From a starting pool of 90 phages, three rounds of selection left just three winners. The team grew them, stripped out bacterial toxins, and ran strict checks: shelf life, sterility, heat-causing impurities, and safety on human cells. Gene and protein scans confirmed the phages kill rather than hide inside their hosts, and carry no toxin genes. Electron microscope images showed the right virus shapes attacking the right bacteria. A pilot trial in patients was already cleared to begin.
europmc-pmc2667253:
Cureton and co-authors filmed in 2009 how a rod-shaped virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, sneaks into cells through a doorway built for much smaller loads. Cells swallow surface material in bubbles coated with a protein called clathrin. The virus is longer than a normal bubble is wide, so full coating looks impossible.

High-resolution movies of single viruses entering lit-up cells showed the answer: part coating is enough. Virus bubbles carried more clathrin than usual, but never a full shell. The missing help came from actin, the cell's moving scaffold, whose parts gathered at the virus bubbles. Blocking actin froze the viruses at the surface, trapped in half-made bubbles. The team also showed the virus triggers its own doorway rather than waiting for a random one to form.
europmc-pmc2669153:
Korolchuk and co-authors showed in 2009 that the cell's two garbage systems back each other up in unexpected ways. One system, the proteasome, shreds proteins tagged with a marker called ubiquitin. The other, autophagy, wraps larger loads and digests them in acid sacs. The two were long thought to serve separate clients.

When the team blocked autophagy in cells, proteasome targets piled up anyway. The cause was a helper protein, p62, which itself builds up when autophagy stops. Extra p62 gums up delivery of tagged proteins to the proteasome, delaying their destruction. Short-lived control proteins such as p53, and clump-prone proteins linked to brain disease, rose as a result. Blocking one system, the authors warn, quietly weakens the other, a fact that matters for drugs aiming at either route.
europmc-pmc2671453:
Meijer and the European Influenza Surveillance Scheme group reported in 2009 that flu viruses able to resist the main flu drug had spread across Europe in the 2007–08 season. The drug, oseltamivir, sold as Tamiflu, was a front-line treatment and preventive for influenza A H1N1. Resistant viruses had once been rare curiosities.

That season they were anything but rare. The scheme ties the spread to two helpers: a heavy season of virus circulation, and the arrival of a changed virus variant in a population with little immunity to it. Resistant strains could ride that wave even though few Europeans took the drug. The report warned health agencies that resistance can take hold without drug pressure, changing how stockpiles and treatment guides should be planned for future seasons and pandemics.
europmc-pmc2699053:
Ma and a large team read in 2009 the genome of Rhizopus oryzae, the fungus behind mucormycosis, a fast, often fatal infection that invades blood vessels. It kills over half its victims. The fungus also serves science as a model of the early-branching fungi, a group whose history was sketchy.

The genome spans 45.3 million letters, about a fifth of it jumping DNA repeats. Among its 13,895 genes, many sit in matched pairs. Their arrangement and shared ancestry point to one ancient event: the whole genome doubled. The doubling copied nearly every part of the cell's energy and waste systems. Gene families for growth signals and for secreted cutting enzymes, known weapons of fungal infection, expanded too. One doubled target of antifungal drugs may explain the species' uneven response to those drugs. The cell wall recipes, absent from human cells, offer clean targets for new ones.
europmc-pmc2706953:
Hewitson, Grainger, and Maizels reviewed in 2009 how helminths, parasitic worms, calm the host immune system with proteins they secrete. Worm infection usually drives a Th2 response, one arm of immunity, while also raising cells that damp immunity down. That mix lets worms live for a long time inside a host.

Clearing worms with drugs reverses the calming effect, which proves live worms actively hold immunity down. Their review surveys single secreted proteins that block host signals at many steps, from first sensing to final attack. Targets include immune messengers and receptors, the docking sites on cells, plus proteins that break down or shield against host defenses.
europmc-pmc2775953:
Liao and co-authors showed in 2009 that cancer-associated fibroblasts drive tumor growth and spread by shaping the immune setting around a tumor, in a mouse model of metastatic breast cancer. Fibroblasts make up most cells in tumor stroma, the supporting tissue, and are tempting drug targets. The team removed them in living mice with a DNA vaccine aimed at fibroblast activation protein, a marker on these cells.

Removing the fibroblasts flipped the local immune balance from a Th2 pattern to a Th1 pattern, the kind that attacks tumors. Protein levels of two immune signals rose, while suppressive cells and new blood and lymph vessels fell. The vaccine also boosted the anti-metastasis effect of doxorubicin chemotherapy and drew in more dendritic cells and killer T cells. Fibroblasts, they conclude, are valid treatment targets in metastatic breast cancer.
europmc-pmc2794253:
Wu and colleagues presented a faster way in 2009 to free living plant cells from their walls, using the small weed Arabidopsis. Such wall-free cells, called protoplasts, let researchers test genes and watch proteins interact inside a living cell. The older method cut leaves into thin slivers, which was slow and often damaged the cells.

Their Tape-Arabidopsis Sandwich sticks one tape to the leaf top and another tape to the underside. Peeling the lower tape strips off the bottom skin, so enzymes can reach the inner cells and digest their walls. Ready protoplasts take under an hour, and gene tests can run within two hours, with less skill and gear needed.
europmc-pmc2798753:
Löffler and colleagues tested in 2010 how strongly a staph toxin called Panton-Valentine leukocidin, or PVL, harms human neutrophils. Neutrophils are white blood cells that rush in first against infection. PVL's role in severe tissue-killing disease was disputed, since mouse studies gave mixed answers.

PVL works by punching pores in the cell membrane. PVL triggered fast activation and death in human and rabbit neutrophils, but left mouse and monkey cells unharmed. Strains releasing PVL killed the cells early and fast, unlike the slower, normal death that follows germ eating. Another staph toxin group hit all species alike. The species gap means mouse and primate models can mislead work on this toxin, the authors warn.
europmc-pmc2829053:
Netea and colleagues reviewed in 2010 how the immune signal IL-1beta gets switched on during infection. IL-1beta and its cousin IL-18 rouse front-line defense cells and steer later adaptive responses, but both are made as inactive precursors that a cutting enzyme must trim. The best-known cutter, caspase-1, is itself switched on by platforms called inflammasomes.

Mice missing caspase-1 or inflammasome parts fall prey to several infections more easily, the review notes. Yet in other infections and in sterile inflammation, caspase-1 matters little. There, enzymes from neutrophils, the first-responder white cells, or even from the germs themselves do the trimming. The authors conclude the inflammasome is one activation route among several, not the whole story.
europmc-pmc2873753:
Chan and co-authors reported in 2003 on Singapore's large 2000 epidemic of hand, foot and mouth disease, a mostly mild childhood illness that can turn deadly. Case reports from doctors and childcare centers showed cases climbing through September and falling by late October. Nearly three thousand eight hundred cases were notified, almost all in children under four years old.

Cultures from patients grew human enterovirus 71 more often than any other virus, in both patients with the illness and patients with other complaints. Five children died, and autopsies on the fatal illness cases showed inflammation of the brain, lungs, and heart muscle. Virus was confirmed in most of the deaths. The account ends with the outbreak plan Singapore built for fast, coordinated control of severe recurrences.
europmc-pmc2913853:
Piccinini and Midwood reviewed in 2010 how the body's own debris, called DAMPs, can keep inflammation burning through the same receptors that detect germs. DAMPs are molecules released by damaged or dying cells, plus matrix fragments freed when tissue is torn. They trip Toll-like receptors, the immune system's alarm sensors, launching repair programs that normally shut off once healing starts.

In rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, and cancer, the alarm instead feeds itself: inflammation damages tissue, damage releases more DAMPs, and the loop becomes chronic. The review distinguishes the signaling routes used by different self-activators, since they are not all equal. Blocking specific DAMPs could calm disease inflammation while leaving germ defense intact, a precision that broad immune suppression cannot offer.
europmc-pmc2914753:
Guerra and colleagues mapped in 2010 the worldwide limits of Plasmodium vivax malaria, the second great human malaria parasite, and counted who lives at risk. Vivax had long been overshadowed by its deadlier cousin, so its true range was fuzzy. They assembled the newest case reports from every endemic country and graded each area as malaria-free, unstable, or stable transmission.

Temperature and aridity layers trimmed the map where the parasite or its mosquitoes cannot persist, and local intelligence erased risk from big cities and free islands inside endemic borders. Overlaying a detailed 2009 population surface gave at-risk headcounts by risk class. The result is a contemporary baseline for the relapsing parasite, whose hidden liver stage makes elimination harder than case counts suggest.
europmc-pmc2923753:
Lenardon, Munro, and Gow reviewed in 2010 chitin synthesis in fungi, the process that builds the skeleton of the fungal cell wall. Chitin is a tough carbohydrate mesh absent from humans and other vertebrates, which makes its machinery an inviting drug target. Fungi place chitin precisely through the cell cycle, reinforcing buds, branches, and the cross-walls that divide cells, and they remodel it fast when the wall is stressed or attacked.

The review assembles how the synthase enzymes are made, shipped, switched on, and restrained, and how those controls fail or adapt during infection of animals and plants. Chitin also talks to the immune system, provoking and at other doses calming responses. Drugs and farm fungicides that jam chitin placement could disarm many pathogens at once, a prospect the authors develop.
europmc-pmc2950153:
Wauquier and colleagues studied blood samples from Ebola patients in Gabon and Congo outbreaks between 1996 and 2003, comparing those who died with those who survived, in a 2010 study. Human immune data on this virus were scarce because outbreaks strike remote areas.

Fatal cases showed floods of inflammatory signalling molecules and growth factors, yet almost none of one key antiviral signal. Their infection-fighting T cells also crashed in number, with death markers rising on the remaining cells, and helper molecules from T cells stayed low. Survivors showed a calmer, better balanced pattern. The profile links death to a misfiring early defence plus immune cell loss.
europmc-pmc3012653:
Hinderliter and colleagues built ISDD, a computer model predicting how many lab-grown cells particles in culture fluid actually reach, in a 2010 article. Toxicity tests usually report dose as what was added to the dish, not what lands on cells, skewing comparisons.

The model combines sinking under gravity with random diffusion for round particles and their clumps. Checked against measured transport for plastic beads of many sizes, silica, and iron oxide clumps, predictions landed close to measurements without any tuning. The authors then chart how particle size, density, and fluid depth change the true cellular dose.
europmc-pmc3035253:
Auch, von Jan, Klenk, and Göker tested in 2010 whether computers can replace a slow lab test used to decide if two microbes belong to one species. The old test mixes DNA from two strains and measures how well it sticks together, but it is tedious, error prone, and cannot build a shared database. Genome sequencing offered a faster path, if the math could match the old results.

The team compared methods that find long matching DNA stretches between two genomes and turn them into a distance score. Their best formulas tracked the old test closely, handled shrunken and repetitive genomes, and stayed steady when parts of a genome were missing. The scores also matched a standard gene based family tree better than the old test did. The methods were released as a web service for naming new species.
europmc-pmc3037053:
Sundar and Chakravarty reviewed in 2010 the harms of antimony, a metal used both in industry and as a medicine. Workers can breathe it in, causing lung irritation, skin spots, and stomach trouble, and one form may cause cancer. As a drug, antimony compounds have long treated two parasitic diseases, leishmaniasis and schistosomiasis.

During treatment, the main dangers are heart rhythm damage, seen in roughly one in eleven patients, and inflammation of the pancreas. The pancreas problem is especially common when patients also carry HIV and visceral leishmaniasis together. Safer workplaces have cut job related cases sharply. For patients, the authors stress checking each drug batch for quality and watching closely for side effects throughout treatment. Careful monitoring keeps a useful old drug acceptably safe.
europmc-pmc3057953:
Philippe and coauthors argued in 2011 that simply gathering more DNA sequences will not settle the hardest questions about the tree of life. Their essay responds to genome scale studies of early animal evolution that reached strongly conflicting trees despite huge datasets. Each rival tree tells a very different story about how simple or complex the first animals were.

The trouble, they argue, is not a lack of data but systematic error inside it. Fast evolving lineages, poor models, and contaminated or misaligned sequences can pull a tree the wrong way with great statistical confidence. More data then makes a wrong answer look more certain, not less. The authors urge better models, careful data selection, and slower thinking over brute volume. Their piece is a caution to a field dazzled by sequencing speed.
europmc-pmc3063653:
Bouvier and Lowen reviewed in 2010 the animal models used to study how influenza viruses cause disease and spread. Human flu ranges from silent infection to fatal pneumonia, depending on the strain and on the person's age, immunity, and past exposures. Not every strain that can infect people can pass between them, which is the property that decides pandemic risk.

Ferrets, mice, guinea pigs, hamsters, cotton rats, and monkeys each copy part of the human picture. Ferrets sneeze and spread virus much like people, while mice allow deep genetic work but spread virus poorly. The review weighs each model's strengths and limits for testing drugs and vaccines before human use. Choosing the right animal for each question, the authors argue, is what turns lab results into reliable warnings about real strains.
europmc-pmc3093253:
Jiao, Yu, Zhang, and Ewart reviewed in 2011 the chemistry and medical promise of sulfated sugars from seaweeds. These long sugar chains, decorated with sulfate groups, are made by red, green, and brown algae and include familiar materials such as carrageenan and agar relatives. Cut into shorter pieces, they show a striking range of biological effects in lab studies.

The review first updates the detailed structures of the main families, which differ by algae type and sugar building blocks. It then surveys their actions: thinning blood and blocking clots, fighting viruses, calming inflammation, lowering blood lipids, and mopping up damaging oxygen radicals. Several effects are strong enough to interest drug developers, though the molecules are complex and hard to standardize. The authors present them as a rich, renewable source of candidate medicines from the sea.
europmc-pmc3120753:
Sven Bocklandt and colleagues built a way to guess age from chemical marks on DNA in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Marks called methylation change steadily across life and affect how genes behave. The team scanned saliva DNA from male identical twins and found dozens of sites whose marking tracked closely with age.

Three sites, near genes involved in growth and nerve signalling, rose or fell in a straight line across five decades of life. Using just two of the sites, the team predicted age with an average error of only a few years. Such a test could help forensic work when only a body sample exists, and could one day flag people ageing faster than their years suggest.
europmc-pmc3175453:
Irene Winkler, Stefan Haufe, and Michael Tangermann built an automatic cleaner for brain-wave recordings in a 2011 paper in Behavioral and Brain Functions. Recordings are polluted by eye, muscle, and device artefacts, and the standard fix, hand-picking bad components after a mathematical separation, is slow and varies by person. Their classifier learns from expert-labelled components instead.

Using just six features spanning frequency, space, and time patterns, the linear classifier matched expert disagreement levels on its training study. It held up well on a new listening study with different equipment. On motor-imagery data it preserved the brain signals a brain-computer interface needs, even while discarding the worst three fifths of components. The method works across headsets and subjects without per-person artefact recordings.
europmc-pmc3218953:
Jennifer Patnaik and colleagues asked what older women with breast cancer actually die of, in this 2011 retrospective study in Breast Cancer Research. Many survivors die of unrelated causes, so the team used a linked cancer-registry and Medicare database. They followed more than sixty thousand women diagnosed at age sixty-six or older between 1992 and 2000.

After a median follow-up of about nine years, just under half the women were still alive. Heart and blood-vessel disease was the single largest cause of death, edging out breast cancer itself. Age and other illnesses at diagnosis drove deaths from other causes most strongly, and conditions such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes also raised breast-cancer mortality somewhat. The authors urge priority for heart-health care in long-term follow-up.
europmc-pmc3221353:
David Mohr, Pim Cuijpers, and Kenneth Lehman proposed a model called Supportive Accountability in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Online health programs work better when a human supports the user, but that support was rarely described or guided by theory. The authors built their model from organizational psychology, motivation research, and studies of computer-mediated communication.

In their account, support works through accountability: users stick with a program when answerable to a coach they see as trustworthy, kind, and expert. Expectations should be clear, focused on process, and set with the patient's input, and the benefits of the relationship should be mutual. Intrinsic motivation reduces how much support a person needs, and the communication channel, phone, email, or messaging, shapes the process. Each part of the model is offered as a testable claim.
europmc-pmc3315253:
Li and Siegrist combined long term studies to measure how physical activity protects the heart, reporting in 2012. They searched three decades of research and kept only large, high quality studies that followed adults free of heart disease for at least five years. Twenty one studies qualified, covering more than six hundred fifty thousand people and about twenty thousand new cases of disease.

People with the most active leisure time had roughly a quarter lower risk of heart and blood vessel disease than the least active, in both men and women. More activity brought steadily more protection. A moderate amount of physical work on the job also helped, cutting risk by a smaller margin. The authors say the pattern supports prevention efforts in rich and developing countries alike.
europmc-pmc3366753:
Keiser and Utzinger warned in 2005 that foodborne trematodiasis — infection with liver, lung, and intestinal flukes — was emerging as a public health problem. People acquire these parasites by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish, crustaceans, or aquatic plants, and the diseases they cause range from liver damage to chronic intestinal illness.

The authors linked the rise chiefly to booming freshwater aquaculture, which expands habitats and distribution routes for the parasites. In China, infections with the liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis had more than tripled in a decade, reaching roughly fifteen million people. They urged that aquaculture expansion in endemic regions be monitored so food production gains do not come with more disease.
europmc-pmc3379953:
Rizzardi and colleagues tested in 2012 whether computers can score tissue staining as reliably as pathologists do by eye. Such staining, called immunohistochemistry, validates markers found by gene studies, but visual scoring is costly and subjective. The team used tissue arrays built from more than two hundred ovarian cancer specimens stained for one protein.

Software first outlined the cancer areas, then measured how much staining they held. Its outlines matched the pathologists' hand-drawn ones closely. Staining scores from pixel analysis tracked the visual scores very tightly on both measures used. The study shows digital scoring can turn a judged grade into a continuous, repeatable number.
europmc-pmc3430553:
Hayes, Hayes, and Mikedis pooled brain-scan studies of posttraumatic stress disorder in 2012 to find the neural pattern that survives across study designs. Scans had implicated many regions, but results varied widely. Their meta-analysis gathered data from several hundred patients and matched controls across dozens of studies published before 2011.

Two zones stood out as overactive in patients: parts of the anterior cingulate and, in targeted studies, the amygdala on both sides. Underactivity spread widely, especially in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and a frontal region nearby. The quieter that prefrontal zone ran, the hotter the amygdala burned, a coupling the authors verified directly. The pattern supports a model of PTSD as a broken balance between salience detection and emotion control.
europmc-pmc3433453:
Pendleton led a team that produced the first global estimate in 2012 of carbon emissions from wrecking vegetated coasts. Marshes, mangroves, and seagrasses lock away huge carbon stores in their sediments, the so-called blue carbon. Earlier counts tallied only the uptake lost when these places vanish, missing the stored carbon that escapes.

Combining world area data, conversion rates, and near-surface carbon stocks, the team estimated yearly releases spanning a wide range, several times the older figures. The total rivals a noticeable share of global deforestation emissions, with yearly damages in the tens of billions of dollars. These emissions sit outside current carbon accounting and markets. Protecting coasts, they conclude, is climate policy hiding in plain sight.

europmc-pmc9936053: Doctors and scientists took on the use of delphi in health sciences research: a narrative review in this 2023 review paper. europmc-pmc9979453: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on CD39/CD73/A2AR pathway and cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
eutropius-abridgment-watson-1853:
Eutropius wrote his Breviarium, a short history of Rome, around 369 CE for the emperor Valens, who wanted the past in brief. John Selby Watson translated it into English in 1853, adding a notice on the author's life. In ten slim books the story runs from Romulus to the emperor Jovian.

Each reign gets a few crisp lines: wars won, lands gained, emperors made and unmade. The plain style made the book a school text for a thousand years, the most copied Roman history of the Middle Ages. Readers who want the whole arc of Rome in one short read still start here.
filmer-advertisement-to-jury-men-english:
Robert Filmer, the royalist thinker, published his Advertisement to the Jury-Men of England in 1653. The tract warns jurors against convicting witches on rotten evidence. Filmer also draws a neat line between the witch of English law and the witch of Hebrew Scripture, arguing the two are not the same.

His caution is legal rather than tender. Bad proofs, he insists, make bad verdicts, whatever the crime. Coming from a defender of kings, the skepticism surprises. The law here questions itself in a quiet voice. Filmer's pamphlet belongs to the slow English retreat from witch convictions, led as much by lawyers' doubts about evidence as by any change of heart.
frus-1861-d153:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 September 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 153 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The crossing habit of the Paris file appears once more in September. Each man wrote from his own week's facts, not the other's. The record gains from it: two honest views of one bond, neither trimmed to fit the last letter. Neither view was trimmed to please the other, which gives the file its force. Force of that kind is why scholars still read this file with close care.
frus-1861-d253:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands, dated 18 September 1861. Congress received it as Document 253 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d53:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 June 1861. It is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams and Seward wrote to each other on the same day more than once that summer. Neither could answer the other's latest word for at least two weeks. Their letters form two lines that cross but never quite meet, a true picture of rule by mail across an ocean. Their crossed letters of June show a bond of trust that distance could not fray. Trust that survives slow mails is the strongest kind a service can build.
frus-1862-d153:
A dispatch of 26 September 1862 from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, as Document 153 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of many Seward letters sent across the Atlantic that fall.

London and Washington were ten days or more apart by mail steamer, so each side often answered news the other had already moved past. That gap shaped the tone of the whole exchange. Short, frequent dispatches like this one kept the envoy supplied with fresh orders and fresh facts as the British cabinet weighed its course. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d253:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 19 February 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 253 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter joined the regular flow between the Department and the Paris legation.

Mid-February 1862 brought the surrender of Fort Donelson, a Union triumph that impressed foreign watchers. Seward could write to Europe from a stronger hand than he had held in months. His letters to Dayton in this season worked that advantage, pressing France to keep its distance from the Confederacy while Union arms advanced. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d353:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to Henri Mercier on 10 January 1862. In a letter printed as Document 353 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier served as the French minister in Washington.

Early January was a settling time after the Trent settlement, with both Britain and France recalculating their American course. French forces were ashore in Mexico, and Washington wanted French aims stated plainly. Seward's letters to Mercier in this season kept the channel warm while harder questions formed behind it. French citizens and ships caught by the war gave the legation a steady stream of case work.
frus-1862-d453:
Six days after his last order to Vienna, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to John Lothrop Motley on 10 March 1862. The dispatch is Document 453 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The quick follow-up is typical of Seward's style: when news moved, instructions moved with it. That week the ironclads Monitor and Merrimack had just fought in Hampton Roads, an event every naval power in Europe studied closely. Motley needed Washington's account of such events before Vienna's court formed its own. Short orders like this one kept American ministers current, and they make the printed file read like the working log of a government at war.
frus-1862-d53:
By the date of 26 April 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 53 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d553:
The Belgian file opens on 17 March 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Brussels. It is Document 553 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Belgium was a small, industrial kingdom whose king, Leopold I, was uncle and adviser to half the courts of Europe. Sanford, a wealthy and energetic Connecticut man, made Brussels a listening post as much as a legation. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Belgian court. The letter begins a file in which a minor post punches above its weight, because Sanford reported everything and knew everyone.
frus-1862-d653:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Townsend Harris in Japan on 7 October 1861. Harris was nearing the end of his time as the first American minister there. The letter is document 653 in the Foreign Relations volume covering 1862.

By the fall of 1861 the Civil War filled Seward's desk, yet the Japan file still drew his care. Letters of this kind kept the legation in line with Washington's plans and told Harris what news from home might mean for his work. It is one piece of the steady stream that held a new and fragile link between the two lands.
frus-1863p1-d153:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 10 April 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 153 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a Seward letter often added the point that had just ripened at home. In April 1863 the ripening news was of the war and of Congress's mood. Adams had to know both to speak well in London. This letter is the second half of the day's work from Washington. Filed with its twin, it keeps the exchange's pace into mid-April.
frus-1863p1-d253:
The State Department's mail for London dated 29 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 253 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d353:
A formal note dated 7 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 353 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Trade bound the countries tightly, from Southern cotton to British mills. Both sides had much to lose from a break, and the notes reflect that caution. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d453:
Document 453 in the volume is a letter of 9 April 1863 from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d53:
Stephen R. Mallory wrote to James M. Mason on 30 October 1862. Mallory was the Confederate secretary of the navy; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 53 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mallory wrote to London twice in this file within the week, a sign of how much of his navy was being built in British yards. Mason was his man on the spot, facing the builders and the British law. This letter is part of that traffic. Read against the Adams mail in the same volume, it shows both sides of one fight. One side sought ships for the South. The other drove to stop them.
frus-1863p1-d553:
Secretary William H. Seward addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 6 June 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d653:
F. W. Seward, the Assistant Secretary of State sent an official note to Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London on 2 November 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d153: On November 21, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, and two more Churchill notes of the same date follow in the volume. This one is Document 153 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three notes in a day, on the eve of a conference both men were attending in person, shows how much still ran on paper. The record gives the date and the names. The text is in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d253:
President Roosevelt's morning calls at Cairo on 23 November 1943 are reconstructed by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The Log lists the visitors: Vyshinsky, Mountbatten, Churchill with his daughter, the Chiangs, and three Chinese generals. No memoranda of the talks were made, so the editors rely on letters from Harriman and Bohlen.

The fullest account concerns Andrey Vyshinsky, who was passing through on his way to serve as the Soviet member of the Advisory Council for Italy. Roosevelt urged close three-power cooperation on that council, aired his troubles with de Gaulle, and floated trusteeship for immature countries, naming Morocco. Vyshinsky agreed in general terms and seemed struck by the President's frankness. The note also weighs when Tehran lodging invitations from Russia and Britain reached Roosevelt.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d353:
The Log of the President's trip continues with the Tehran chapter, covering 27 November to 2 December 1943. Kept hour by hour by Lieutenant William Rigdon, it opens with a fog-delayed departure from Cairo on the morning of 27 November.

The President's plane took off at seven minutes past seven. It flew 1,310 miles in about six and a half hours. The route passed over the Suez Canal and circled Jerusalem for the view. It then followed the Lend-Lease road and rail lines across Iraq and Iran. Trainloads of supplies bound for Russia could be seen from the air. The party landed at Gale Morghe airport, a Russian army field south of Tehran, with no honors, by request, for security. General Connolly met the President, who drove straight to the American Legation.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d453: Inserted at Document 453, an editorial note carries the historians' voice. The Cairo-Tehran volume collects papers from the 1943 summit conferences. Its editors added notes where context was missing from the file. A note might explain an earlier decision or cite a parallel record. Cairo hosted talks before and after the Tehran meeting with Stalin. Keeping those stages straight is part of the note's work here.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d53: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on October 22, 1943, the day after their previous exchange in this series. The letter is Document 53 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Replies at a day's turn were the rhythm of their wartime partnership. The record states sender, receiver, and date, and offers no subject line. In the published volume it sits with the other papers written while the foreign ministers met in Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d553:
President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin on February 23, 1944, keeping up the direct correspondence the two men had begun before they ever met. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume, in its follow-up section.

By February the Red Army was advancing fast, and the questions between Washington and Moscow mixed military coordination with the first hard problems of Poland and the postwar map. Roosevelt's letters to Stalin worked to hold the partnership steady through those strains. For readers, this message belongs to the testing season of the alliance, when Tehran's goodwill met the realities of armies moving west.
frus-1944-quebec-d153:
British strategy for the war against Japan is set out in this chiefs of staff memorandum of August 23, 1944. Since the Sextant Conference, American forces had raced across the Pacific, Japan had reinforced Burma to ten divisions, and Germany's possible collapse might soon free troops. London had studied how British forces could best help finish the Pacific war.

The paper rejects continuing the slog in North Burma, where sickness alone cost 282,000 casualties in early 1944. Instead it backs Mountbatten's Vanguard plan: seize Rangoon by airborne assault and cut Japan's communications in Burma. It also offers a strong British fleet, built around new battleships and carriers, to serve under American command in the main operations against Japan by mid-1945.
frus-1944-quebec-d253:
Roosevelt answered Stettinius from Quebec on September 15, 1944, and the compromise voting formula found no favor. Neither he nor Churchill was inclined to approve the proposed amendment. Roosevelt's own thought was to record the subject in the Dumbarton Oaks agreement as discussed but undecided, leaving it to the meeting of the United Nations.

Churchill feared that course would be unacceptable to the Russians. They would know they faced overwhelming defeat in a United Nations meeting, grow sore, and take it out on the allies on some other point. Roosevelt counseled keeping on trying. Failing agreement, he preferred silence about the disagreement, or a general statement that certain points remained open. The editors note both London and Moscow soon rejected the formula officially.
frus-1944-quebec-d53:
Lester B. Pearson, Canada's ambassador in Washington, wrote to Harry Hopkins on September 3, 1944. Pearson, later Canada's prime minister, was then his country's chief envoy to the United States. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Canada was host to the coming conference and a full partner in the war, and Pearson's channel to Hopkins handled the Canadian side of the arrangements from Washington. A message in this channel shows the host country working quietly inside the alliance's machinery. For readers, it adds a diplomat of future fame to the conference's supporting cast.
frus-1945-50-intel-d153:
A memorandum dated 6 June 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Langer). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Staff Committee. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 153 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d253:
Dated 9 December 1947, this memorandum runs from the Executive Secretary (Souers) to the Members of the National Security Council. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 253, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d353:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached Allen W. Dulles on 17 November 1948. Readers meet it as document 353 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles survey team was checking how well the CIA worked, and agencies across Washington were stating their views on the record.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d53:
Rear Admiral Thomas Inglis, chief of naval intelligence, wrote to Admiral King, chief of naval operations, on 30 November 1945. The paper moved inside the Navy's own chain. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Naval intelligence had won great victories in the war, above all in code-breaking, and its chief meant to keep its strength and secrets. Inglis reported to the one man whose backing he most needed. Readers meet the Navy thinking as a service here, distinct from Forrestal's cabinet-level maneuvering. The two levels, the uniformed chief and the secretary, worked the same cause from different chairs, and the volume lets readers watch both at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d153:
From Warm Springs on 15 December 1944, Roosevelt asked Churchill what to do next about Poland. His top secret telegram, number 674, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the prime minister's Commons statement on the Polish question.

Roosevelt wants Churchill's judgment on two things. First, can Mikolajczyk come back into power with enough authority to carry out his plans? Second, what should the allies do if the Lublin Committee declares itself Poland's provisional government and Stalin recognizes it? He wonders whether to ask Stalin to hold off any firm step until the three leaders meet. Pressure at home, he adds, may force him to publish the policy points of his letter to Mikolajczyk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d253:
Stalin argued for an invasion through Switzerland at a Moscow military conference, Harriman reported on 15 October 1944. His account to the President, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, covers the previous night's session. General Brooke, backed by Churchill, had laid out the allied plans.

Stalin called the attack on the Ruhr the knockout blow for Germany, yet again urged turning the Siegfried Line from the south, through Switzerland. Churchill explained why that move would not work, and voiced confidence in the drive in the north. On Italy, Stalin showed keen interest in landings on the Istrian peninsula, and in allied and Soviet forces joining hands in Austria. General Antonov then gave the Red Army's position, starting with an offensive in the far north, two miles from Petsamo.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d353:
Alger Hiss filled pages with pencil notes during the February 6, 1945 plenary at Livadia Palace. His jottings open with errands — a note to the President, pictures to be sent, a redraft on voting — then list who sat where. The three delegations are named man by man, down to the interpreters standing behind the chairs.

The substance follows in shorthand bursts. Stettinius reported that "and the dismemberment" would be added to Article XII of the surrender terms. Molotov withdrew a further proposal of his own. Churchill said his Cabinet had not approved the instrument, yet he welcomed the agreement. Hiss shows the session as a staffer lived it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d453:
Hiss's jottings of February 10, 1945, follow Eden's report on Poland to the plenary. Agreement had been reached, Eden said, with two questions outstanding. He read the draft as it then stood. It carried changes agreed by Churchill and Stettinius in a private meeting before the session, plus Molotov's noon amendment.

A new amendment appears in the notes: the powers would exchange ambassadors, by whose reports their governments would keep informed about Poland. Churchill then spoke on frontiers. All were agreed on the eastern frontier, and in principle on the western. The Poles were to have East Prussia and freedom to go to the Oder line. Hiss shows the formula closing, clause by clause.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d53: Roosevelt closed this opening run of papers with a message to Churchill on 12 January 1945. It is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Days later the president sailed for the Mediterranean, and the written preparation in these fifty-three documents gave way to the conferences themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d153:
Secretary of State Stettinius raised the idea of a joint surrender demand on Japan in a telegram from San Francisco dated June 15, 1945. The message to Grew is document 153 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Joint Chiefs had reported that Japan might seek to end the war on certain terms.

Stettinius asks whether the demand for unconditional surrender should be made a three- or four-power demand, issued at or after the Big Three meeting. It might be paired with some assurances to the Japanese about their future. Getting Russia to join such a demand would be worth a real effort, he argues. If a demand is needed when the Okinawa fighting ends, the President should issue it alone, in a way that does not block later Big Three action. The idea led toward the Potsdam Declaration issued that July.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d253:
A briefing paper laid out Korea's future in three stages, dated July 4, 1945. The paper is document 253 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is a companion to the paper on interim administration printed just before it in the volume.

The first stage is an Allied military government, with Allied representation in the occupation army and its administration so far as practicable. The second is an interim international supervisory administration, running Korea until the Koreans can govern themselves. The third is a free and independent Korea, as the Cairo Declaration promised. The Department's recommendations are stated in three short paragraphs, one for each stage. In the event, the middle stage never came: Korea was divided at the 38th parallel instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d353:
How the Reparations Commission and the Control Council should share power is mapped in a Joint Civil Affairs Committee memorandum. American policy, set down for Pauley's guidance in Moscow, made the occupation authorities responsible for carrying out the reparations plan inside Germany. The two bodies were not to work at cross purposes.

Within that rule, the Control Council could hold back specific items from transfer as reparations. It could act when removal would cut Germany's means below the least level the occupation's other aims required. If the Council split, a zone commander who believed an item should stay could carry the question higher. The memo guards German recovery against reparations demands.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d453:
Hayter, secretary general of the British delegation, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945, with news on the Greek elections. Since his letter of the night before, the Foreign Office had heard that the Greek government agreed to the proposals put to it in Athens. The way was therefore open for invitations.

Invitations could now go to the Soviet and French governments. The Foreign Office suggested the invitation to the Russians be made to their representatives at the conference on July 17 or 18. That timing should allow a Soviet reply before the conference, called Terminal, ended. The invitation to France could be made in Paris on the same day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d53:
Churchill gave in on the meeting date in telegram number 75 to President Truman, sent from London on June 6, 1945. The printed extract is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. For days Churchill had argued that July 15 was too late for the Big Three to meet near Berlin.

The whole surviving text is one line: Churchill accepts July 15 and is telling Stalin. Truman had told him a day earlier that no earlier date was possible, and the Prime Minister dropped his push for June or early July. With that, the last of the three leaders fell into line, and planning for the Potsdam Conference could go forward on an agreed date.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d553:
Harold Shantz, the U.S. charge in Belgrade, wired the Acting Secretary of State on July 7, 1945. His secret report is document 553 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the state of politics inside Yugoslavia that summer.

Shantz says there is no free press and no free political life. The secret police act as they please, so freedom from fear is lacking too. He reports that Ivan Subasic, the deputy premier, is glad that civil courts are starting. Yet Subasic fears the leaders have lost grip on their own men below. Subasic had asked that Tito be told the Tito-Subasic deal was not being kept. He hoped the Big Three meeting would say so in public.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d653:
The British Embassy in Washington delivered an aide-memoire on Tangier on June 20, 1945. It is document 653 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its subject is how and when to tell the Soviet government about the coming Tangier talks.

London agrees with Washington that the time to inform Moscow has now come. Tangier, it notes, has lately drawn much press attention. Britain holds that France should be joined with any message to the Soviets on the talks. It proposes that the British and U.S. embassies in Paris approach the French foreign ministry together. A draft cable is attached, setting out the lines the message to Moscow should follow. The short paper shows the care taken to keep Moscow informed, but at arm's length.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1053: Secretary of War Henry Stimson included this passage in his memorandum to President Truman of July 16, 1945. The printed text is an extract; the rest appears elsewhere in the volume. Stimson says he would grant Poland some areas on her western border. They would offset the territory Poland is to cede to Russia in the east. His condition concerns the Germans living in those western areas. Russia, he insists, must show that proper care will be made for those millions. They must not be shunted onto American responsibility.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1153:
James Clement Dunn, an assistant secretary of state on the American team, wrote this memorandum on 31 July 1945. Dunn was a career diplomat of long service. His papers summed up staff judgment for the team's leaders in the summit's last round.

A note written two days before the close belongs to the work of finishing: fixing stands, noting what remained open, and preparing the record. Dunn's view is the trained envoy's, not the politician's. His memoranda across the volume show how the American machine thought as it worked. This one catches it at the finish line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1253:
The Secretary of State wrote to Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov on 26 July 1945. Byrnes to Molotov was the working channel between the American and Soviet chiefs at Potsdam. The two men handled much of the summit's hardest business between themselves.

A letter on this channel could press a point, propose a text, or register a stand for the record. This one went out the day the Allied terms to Japan were issued and Britain changed leaders. It shows the American chief tending the Soviet tie on the summit's fullest day. The paper joins the set of Byrnes-Molotov exchanges that carried the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1353:
Joseph Grew, the acting secretary of state, wrote to Secretary Byrnes at Potsdam on 19 July 1945. Grew's letters crossed the Atlantic throughout the conference, keeping the secretary tied to his department. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

These home-office letters did quiet but vital work: they told the men abroad what Congress, the press, and other agencies were doing in Washington. A secretary cut off from that flow would have bargained half blind. This second Grew letter in the run shows the channel in steady use. It rounds out the picture of a department split between two cities for a month.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-153:
Another delegation memorandum bears the date July 31, 1945, the eve of the Potsdam close. The volume holds a cluster of staff papers from that day. Each one moved a small piece of the ending into place. This memo was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Clustered papers reveal the division of labor at the end. While leaders met, officers chased the details that made agreement real. The memorandum preserves one such chase in writing. Readers studying the final protocol can use papers like this to see its roots. They show the settlement as work, not just words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-53:
An editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers covers a visit by Secretary Stimson to Churchill on July 21, 1945. No official record of the conversation has been found, the editors say. In its place they print Stimson's diary entry for that day.

Stimson writes that he left the Little White House and picked up Harvey Bundy on the way. At the prime minister's house they conferred with Churchill and Lord Cherwell. Stimson turned over a paper to Churchill, who began reading it on the spot. A few minutes before five, Churchill was interrupted and had to hurry to the Big Three conference. He asked Stimson to return the following morning to finish up the report. The paper is identified by the editors as document 1305, the fuller report in the atomic series printed later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d753:
Artemus Gates, Under Secretary of the Navy, wrote to a senior fleet plans officer on July 21, 1945. Document 753 is a Navy house paper from the Potsdam week. It passed between the Navy's civilian head and the staff of the Commander in Chief, United States Fleet. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

Service papers like this one show the war machine's inner mail. Civilian chiefs and uniformed planners traded views in plain terms. Readers see naval concerns carried at a high level while the summit sat. The document widens the volume beyond diplomats: fleets, too, had a stake in what Potsdam decided.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d853:
Document 853 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 18, 1945. Staff drafted it on the conference's second day. Early working papers turned briefing books into live texts. This one stayed in the delegation files and entered the second Potsdam volume.

Second-day drafts show a team settling to its work. The writers now had the other sides' tones in their ears. Readers can look for early adjustments in the paper's lines. The document belongs to the foundation layer of the talks. Before the famous clashes came days of quiet drafting, and this paper is a piece of that groundwork.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d953:
Soviet delegates handed this reparations proposal to Secretary Byrnes on July 30, 1945, though the paper itself is undated. Each government would take one-time removals from its own zone within two years of the surrender. The removals should speed rebuilding in countries that suffered under German occupation, and cut Germany's war potential.

Because Soviet heavy industry suffered huge losses, the USSR also claims 5.5 to 6 million tons of listed equipment from the western zones, mainly the Ruhr. It further claims company shares worth 500 million dollars. Yearly deliveries of current goods would total 8 billion dollars over ten years, half going to the USSR.
frus-1961-63v11-d53: Another 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the Missile Crisis volume. The crisis papers. This document holds that memo. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. The text survives intact.
frus-1969-76v02-d53: A 1969-1976 FRUS memorandum from President Nixon to the Secretary. The president wrote. This document preserves that memo. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
galileo-sidereus-nuncius-1653:
Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius, The Starry Messenger, appears here in the 1653 London Latin printing. Galileo published the work in Latin in 1610, reporting what his improved telescope showed. No public-domain English translation exists for this line, so the text stands in Latin, as early readers across Europe read it.

Galileo reported mountains on the Moon, four moons circling Jupiter, and crowds of stars inside the Milky Way. Each sight struck the old picture of perfect, unchanging heavens. News of the book raced across Europe and made Galileo famous and suspect at once. The slim 1610 report, kept here in its 1653 London form, is one of the founding documents of modern astronomy.
gao-gaoreports-b-297553: Bio-Rad Laboratories took its February 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Lab giants get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297853: The Castle Group took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-306353: The Capitol architect's contract ratification got a fiscal ruling in this October 2005 GAO call, which tests the ratification. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the ratification was legal. The law had the final word. The ratification had to be legal.
gao-gaoreports-b-310553: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Comprehensive Health Services, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-311453: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by L-3 Communications EOTech, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-400153: This 2008 GAO ruling is about agency Tender Official at Gary M. Williamson. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions. The full text sits with this description in the library.
