Soline Lacour, Emmanuelle Bechet, Alain Cozzone and co-authors studied a bacterial kinase crossroads in E. coli in 2008. A new class of bacterial enzymes called BY-kinases adds phosphate to tyrosine, much as eukaryotic kinases do, yet they share no structure with them. Only a few of their targets were known.

One target is UDP-glucose dehydrogenase, an enzyme tied to making colanic acid, a protective coating. Its phosphorylation sits at the crossroads of coating synthesis and polymyxin resistance, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, that junction links surface building to antibiotic defense in one step.
plos-pone-0003153:
Didem Göz, Keith Studholme, Douglas A. Lappi and colleagues test how light sets the body clock in mice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some responses to light do not form images. One is the syncing of daily rhythms to day and night. These responses use the classic rods and cones. They also use a small set of retinal ganglion cells that sense light themselves through melanopsin.

The team destroyed those light-sensitive ganglion cells in a targeted way with a saporin conjugate. They then measured how the effects of light on mouse circadian rhythms changed. Readers learn how much this rare cell type matters for the clock. The study helps separate image vision from light sensing for timekeeping.
plos-pone-0003253:
Charalambos Kaittanis and co-authors design tiny magnetic sensors to test germs in blood in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Bacterial infections are rising worldwide, and more germs now resist many drugs. The team built sensors from iron oxide nanoparticles, tiny bits that respond to magnets. Their aim was to judge fast which drugs still work on a germ.

The sensors track bacterial activity by magnetic relaxation, shifts in how the bits settle in a field. Readers get a fast test that works in blood samples. A quick answer can cut the days a sick patient spends on the wrong drug.
plos-pone-0003353:
K. Yoong Lim, Douglas E. Soltis, Pamela S. Soltis and colleagues study chromosome change in young polyploid plants in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Polyploidy, often called whole genome duplication, is a major force in evolution of many eukaryotes. Most angiosperm species have undergone at least one round of polyploidy in their history. Despite great progress in understanding much of this, rapid changes were still being traced.

The team examine rapid chromosome evolution in recently formed polyploids in Tragopogon, in the aster family. Readers watch genome doubling swap chromosome parts within a few generations. Tragopogon polyploids formed in historical time, making evolution open to watch as it happens.
plos-pone-0003453:
Penghua Yang and co-authors made drug-producing cattle in this 2008 cloning paper. Their goal was human lactoferrin, a useful milk protein, made at large scale. Older methods of farming such proteins in animals were slow and weak. The team used a new transgenic cloning procedure in cattle.

The cows' mammary glands then served as living bioreactors. Their milk carried functional human lactoferrin. Making medicine in milk could beat factory cell cultures on scale. The paper reports a step toward herds that produce biopharmaceuticals. Large mammal cloning stayed hard and costly, which makes each working drug herd notable for the field.
plos-pone-0003553:
Florian Geier and co-authors modeled plant stem cell control in this 2008 paper. Plants keep pools of flexible stem cells for their whole lives. Those pools sit in meristems, the growing points of shoots and roots. The reference plant Arabidopsis has a well-mapped shoot meristem.

Their quantitative and dynamic model captures how that pool is regulated. It follows signals that balance renewal against differentiation. The equations describe a strategy for never running out of fresh cells. Growers and breeders rely on the same meristem rules. Meristem rules also decide crop size, since flowers and grain start there.
plos-pone-0003653:
François-Denis Desgorces, Geoffroy Berthelot, Nour El Helou, and colleagues published this sports study in PLOS ONE in 2008. They traced best performances in ten famous outdoor events, some dating back to the 1800s. The set runs from the Oxford-Cambridge boat race to the channel swim and beyond.

Across these events, records rose for long stretches and then slowed as they neared bodily limits. The authors argue that the body's own limits, rather than training or will, now set the ceiling. The work maps where human performance in classic endurance events is likely to stall.
plos-pone-0003753:
Cuilin Zhang, Chunfang Qiu, Frank B. Hu, and colleagues published this pregnancy study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Vitamin D levels vary widely among pregnant women. The blood marker 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the standard way to gauge them. The team asked whether a mother's level relates to diabetes in pregnancy.

They measured the marker in maternal plasma and compared it with the risk of gestational diabetes mellitus. Their analysis links the mother's vitamin D state to her odds of developing the condition. The finding adds a nutritional thread to the story of blood sugar trouble in pregnancy.
plos-pone-0003853:
Carmen Palacios, Erik Zettler, Ricardo Amils, and colleagues published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The Río Tinto in Spain is an acid river system of natural, ancient origin, unlike acid mine drainage. Microbes from all three domains of life flourish in its extreme waters, with bacteria running most processes.

The team tested rival hypotheses for how such microbial communities assemble. Patchy chemistry along the river let them weigh environment against dispersal. Their reconciling account shows how both forces can shape who lives where in one of Earth's strangest rivers.
plos-pone-0003953:
Michael A. Schillaci, Howard Waitzkin, Tom Sharmen, and co-authors tracked child vaccination in New Mexico in 2008. Shots are a core part of children's primary care. New Mexico is a poor, largely rural state. It has at times struggled to keep childhood immunization rates up.

Their PLOS ONE article evaluated state rates from 1996 to 2006. It focused on shifts in Medicaid enrollment during those years. Medicaid covers many children whose shots public programs track. The study shows how insurance churn can shake a state vaccination program. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004053:
Lu Feng, Peter R. Reeves, Ruiting Lan, and co-authors redated the cholera family tree in 2008. Cholera has erupted from South Asia in seven pandemics. Local outbreaks also struck between the sixth and seventh pandemics. All pandemic strains belong to serotype O1 of Vibrio cholerae.

Their PLOS ONE article recalibrated the molecular clock for those strains. The new timing supports independent origins for the pandemic clones. Separate origins change how the disease's history is told. They also shape guesses about where the next pandemic clone may arise. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004153:
Emily Holmes and colleagues published this proposal paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Flashbacks, vivid unwanted memories that feel like reliving the event, are the hallmark symptom of posttraumatic stress disorder. Good treatments exist for the full disorder, but early steps to stop it forming are lacking.

The authors propose a cognitive vaccine: a task done soon after trauma that blocks flashbacks from building up. Their candidate is the computer game Tetris, whose visual demands may compete with the brain's recording of traumatic images. The paper lays out the science behind the idea and how it could be tested as an early aid after trauma.
plos-pone-0004253:
Vincent Paupe and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Friedreich ataxia begins with a shortage of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein, and the shortage kills a subset of neurons. Hallmarks of the disease include low activity of iron-sulfur cluster proteins and a weakened defence against oxidative stress.

The team focused on Nrf2, a master switch of that antioxidant defence. They report that Nrf2 fails to move into the nucleus properly, which undermines the oxidative stress response. A switch stuck outside the control room explains why defences stay off even when they are needed.
plos-pone-0004353:
Anne-Cécile Petit and Jean-François Nicolas published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Understanding how embryos build their structures is a central issue in developmental biology. It is essential for interpreting the massive molecular data now available. In the mouse embryo, watching cell behaviour over the long term is difficult.

The team performed a large-scale clonal analysis, tracing the descendants of single cells in the surface ectoderm. They reveal unexpected complexity in how this outer layer takes shape. Lineage maps like this show the embryo is built by more intricate cell movements than textbooks suggest. Each traced clone is one cell's family story.
plos-pone-0004453:
Blood levels of four proteins at the moment of birth are compared in normal pregnancies and in pre-eclampsia by Aparna Reddy, Sangeeta Suri, Ian Sargent, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pre-eclampsia is a dangerous rise in blood pressure during pregnancy. Levels of several proteins, with names like activin A, inhibin A, sFlt-1, and endoglin, climb before the illness starts.

The team measured all four in mothers' blood at delivery, when babies were born. They compared values in healthy pregnancies with those in pre-eclampsia cases. There are also signs of oxidative stress, a kind of chemical wear, in this illness. Clear numbers at birth help doctors judge how the proteins behave at the peak of disease, and whether they can warn of trouble sooner.
plos-pone-0004553:
The origin of a repeated DNA stretch that causes a rare movement disorder is traced by Teresa Almeida, Isabel Alonso, Sandra Martins, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disorder is spinocerebellar ataxia type 10, an inherited neurodegenerative disease marked by poor balance and seizures. It is caused by a large expansion of an ATTCT repeat in the ATXN10 gene.

The first families reported with the disease were of Mexican origin. The team asked where the expansion first arose, its ancestral origin. Tracing a mutation's birthplace explains how it spread and which populations should be offered testing. It also helps separate one founder event from several independent ones, a distinction that shapes genetic counseling for families at risk.
plos-pone-0004653:
Genes that shape how people smoke are hunted in two genome-wide studies at once by Neil Caporaso, Fangyi Gu, Nilanjan Chatterjee, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Smoking behaviors, such as how much a person smokes and how hard quitting is, run partly in families. The contribution of common genetic variation to those behaviors was investigated in a joint analysis.

The data came from two genome-wide association studies within a cancer genetics project, covering more than two thousand men. Pooling studies raises the power to find small genetic effects. Genes found this way can reveal the brain pathways behind nicotine dependence. That knowledge feeds both prevention and the design of drugs to help people quit.
plos-pone-0004753:
Fabio Demontis and Christian Dahmann described the fly version of a human deaf blindness gene, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Usher syndrome is the most common inherited cause of deaf blindness in humans. Deafness in the syndrome comes from disordered hair bundles in the inner ear that sense sound.

The most severe form links to genes for motor and scaffold proteins. The team characterized the fly match of one such gene, called Sans. Flies offer fast genetics to test what the protein does in sensory cells. That may clarify how ear bundles are built and held. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004853:
Hui-Ju Hsu, Chin-Fu Lee, and Roland Kaunas built a dynamic stochastic model of stress fiber alignment under cyclic stretch, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Actin stress fibers are mechanosensitive elements responding to forces affecting morphology, migration, transduction, and function. Cells are internally stressed so fibers extend beyond unloaded lengths, and fibers self adjust their leaning in response to repeated mechanical stretching of substrates.

Stochastic dynamics reproduce frequency dependent alignment patterns. Cells avoid stretch by reorienting fibers predictably. Modeling mechanosensing aids tissue engineering. Vessels and lungs face similar cycles. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004953:
Malaria during pregnancy is a leading cause of death. It endangers mothers and infants alike. Infected red blood cells gather in the placenta. Immune cells gather there too, but the molecular steps behind damage are unclear. Andrea Conroy and colleagues studied one immune signal, C5a. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The tests were done in vitro.

C5a enhanced the disordered inflammatory response to malaria. It also enhanced abnormal blood-vessel growth. That overdrive may help explain placental damage. The results point to C5a as a possible treatment target. Blocking it might protect pregnancies where malaria is common.
plos-pone-0005053:
Cell membranes contain tiny raft zones rich in cholesterol. A fat called sphingomyelin was thought to be cholesterol's main raft partner. Michal Grzybek and colleagues challenged that picture in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied an inner-leaflet fat, a form of phosphatidylethanolamine. Their tool was Langmuir-Blodgett monolayers, single layers of fat on water.

The raft-associated fat interacted with cholesterol comparably to sphingomyelin. The classic model confined rafts to the outer leaflet. This result widens the cast of raft builders. Rafts may exist on both sides of the membrane. That matters because rafts organize signaling proteins. A fuller picture changes how membrane organization is modeled.
plos-pone-0005153:
Estradiol is the main estrogen hormone. It does many jobs in neurons. Olga Varea and colleagues found another in PLOS ONE in 2009. They showed estradiol activates beta-catenin dependent transcription in neurons. Beta-catenin is a messenger in a classic growth pathway. The hormone usually works by binding estrogen receptors. Those receptors then bind DNA directly.

This route is different. The hormone plugs into the beta-catenin gene program. That program shapes how brain cells grow and connect. The finding links estrogen to developmental signaling in the brain. It may help explain estrogen's effects on mood and cognition. It also widens the list of hormone actions. Receptors are not the whole story.
plos-pone-0005253:
Amoeba-like cells crawl by pushing out finger-like extensions called pseudopodia. With no outside cues, they still tend to keep moving in one direction rather than jittering randomly. Bosgraaf and Van Haastert examined that ordered movement in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team showed the extensions are laid down in an ordered pattern, not by chance alone. That built-in persistence lets cells disperse over larger areas. Understanding the pattern helps explain how immune cells and other crawlers explore tissue even without a scent trail to follow. Cells that wander with a plan, not by chance, can cover ground fast, which is why wounds close and why some cancer cells spread so well.
plos-pone-0005353:
A growth factor called rhGM-CSF boosts white blood cell production and is normally given by injection. No clinical report of giving it by mouth existed. Zhang and colleagues ran a single-dose crossover trial of the oral form in healthy volunteers in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Volunteers received the protein by mouth in a randomized, open-label design with two periods. The trial demonstrated the bioavailability of the oral dose, as the abstract states. A pill form would spare patients repeated injections, if later trials confirm the early result. Most proteins are digested in the gut, so a pill form of a protein drug is a surprise worth a close look. And the trial design used here gives a clean first read on it.
plos-pone-0005453:
Chloë James and colleagues studied how a major class of antibiotics enters bacteria, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Germs that resist many drugs are a growing danger in hospitals. Before a drug can kill a germ, it must first cross the germ's outer wall.

Drugs called beta-lactams cross through pore proteins in that wall. The team watched single pores to see how the drugs pass and what slows them down. Knowing the exact path helps chemists design drugs that slip in faster and helps explain how germs shut the door on them.
plos-pone-0005553:
Carola Engler and co-authors presented a one-pot method for joining DNA parts in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Building new genes often means stitching many DNA pieces into a carrier in the right order. Older methods needed many steps and days of work.

Their method, called Golden Gate shuffling, joins at least nine pieces at once in a single tube. Most of the clones it produced held the exact build the team wanted. A fast, reliable joining method speeds all kinds of gene work, from basic research to building microbes that make useful products.
plos-pone-0005653:
Holly Jones and Oswald Schmitz challenged gloomy forecasts about damaged ecosystems in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Reports on the world environment describe deep harm to the systems that support human life. They often predict that recovery, if it comes at all, will take centuries.

The authors reviewed real cases where damaged systems were left or helped to recover. Many bounced back within decades, far faster than the forecasts suggest. That hopeful evidence does not excuse damage, but it strengthens the case for restoration work. Fast recovery cases also show which parts of a system return first and which need active replanting or restocking.
plos-pone-0005753:
Alessandro Achilli and co-authors traced the roots of domestic cattle in 2009 through mitochondrial DNA. Most accounts place cattle domestication in the Fertile Crescent, from local wild aurochs. Some had proposed that European wild cattle also added genes later.

The team surveyed a large set of cattle mitochondrial genomes for signs of mixed origin. The DNA record supports a more layered story than a single birthplace. Knowing where cattle genes came from helps protect rare breeds and their unique traits. It also shows how early farmers spread and blended herds as farming moved across continents.
plos-pone-0005853:
Irina Tcherepanova and co-authors zeroed in 2009 on the single building block of an HIV protein that gives it immune-suppressing power. As AIDS progresses, the blood's cytokine balance flips from a fighting Th1 pattern to a weaker Th2 one. The viral protein Vpr helps drive that flip by suppressing IL-12.

One conserved residue, at position 90, proved key to that suppression. A single letter in one protein steering immunity is a striking target. Changing or blocking that spot might restore a stronger response. The finding sharpens how researchers think about Vpr as a virulence factor.
plos-pone-0005953:
Glioblastoma cells pour out large amounts of glutamate, a signal chemical that can kill nearby brain cells. Dannis van Vuurden, Maryam Yazdani, Ingeborg Bosma and colleagues asked in 2009 how the tumor cells survive their own flood. Their PLOS ONE study looks at AMPA receptors, the cell gates that glutamate opens.

Too much signal through those gates lets harmful ions pour in and can kill the cell. The tumor's answer is to turn its AMPA receptors down, the team reports. That self-defense lets cancer cells thrive in a toxic bath of their own making, and it shows one way a brain tumor clears space around itself to grow.
plos-pone-0006053:
A blood test for cancer might read patterns, not single markers. Yifat Merbl, Royi Itzchak, Tal Vider-Shalit and colleagues tested that systems idea in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper measures natural autoantibodies, the low-level antibodies everyone carries against the body's own parts, and asks whether their broad pattern separates healthy mice from mice bearing tumors.

Large-scale patterns did tell the two apart, the title reports. The usual view prizes strong, targeted antibodies and treats weak ones as noise. Reading the whole pattern instead turns that noise into a signal. The approach could one day help spot tumors early, when treatment has its best chance.
plos-pone-0006153:
Airway muscle is not a bystander in allergy; it carries the allergy receptor itself. Naresh Redhu, Ali Saleh, Lianyu Shan and colleagues asked in 2009 what sets that receptor's level. Their PLOS ONE paper studies human airway smooth muscle cells, which express the high affinity IgE receptor, and tests how proinflammatory and Th2 cytokines regulate the receptor and IgE-dependent activation.

Cytokines of both camps tune the receptor, which in turn governs how strongly the muscle answers IgE. A muscle cell that can raise its own allergy switch helps explain asthma's tightening grip during inflammation. The findings mark the airway muscle as a drug target in its own right, not just a victim of immune signals.
plos-pone-0006253:
Local communities can protect nearby fisheries, but oceans connect every scale of management. Richard Cudney-Bueno and Xavier Basurto examined community-based fisheries management in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Reserves and local rules are widely promoted against overfishing, yet experts disagree on how well they work.

Missing links between local, regional, and national levels reduced the robustness of the system, the title reports. When shocks arrive, unlinked levels cannot back each other up. The study uses the tragedy of the commons as a backdrop, not a verdict. Its lesson: local effort needs wider support to last.
plos-pone-0006353:
Depression is still diagnosed from reported symptoms, with no brain-based test to guide treatment. Sergi Costafreda and colleagues asked whether brain structure itself carries diagnostic or prognostic value in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Depression brings persistent low mood or loss of pleasure, plus behavioural and cognitive disturbance.

The team tested structural neuroanatomy for clues to diagnosis and outcome. A biological marker could make treatment choices more objective. Even partial prediction would help match patients to therapies sooner. The study weighs promise against the limits of single scans. Brain scans alone will not make the call, but they may one day add a useful clue.
plos-pone-0006453:
Tobias Müller and co-authors studied serotonin as an immune signal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Serotonin, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine, is best known for its roles in the brain and nerves. It is also a strong modulator of the immune system. Many immune cells carry serotonin receptors, including dendritic cells, which help start immune responses.

The team tested how serotonin changes dendritic cell behavior in dishes and in living animals. They measured cell migration, release of cytokines and chemokines, and how well the cells prime T cells. The results tie a mood-related chemical to core immune steps. That link could matter for drugs that act on serotonin.
plos-pone-0006553:
Anke Hammer and co-authors recorded brain responses in obsessive-compulsive disorder for PLOS ONE in 2009. The anterior cingulate cortex is thought to be overactive in patients with OCD. That overactivity may reflect an enhanced action monitoring system, a brain alarm that will not quiet down. The team studied brain potentials of conflict and error likelihood.

They compared patients after errorful and errorless learning. Error monitoring is central to OCD symptoms like checking and doubt. Brain potentials offer a direct window on that monitoring in action. Differences between learning styles may point to better training-based therapies.
plos-pone-0006653:
Raffaella Santoro and co-authors tuned ribosomal RNA genes to boost protein output in PLOS ONE in 2009. Picking mammalian cell lines that make large amounts of protein is a major challenge for the drug industry. Ribosomal RNA genes code for core parts of ribosomes, the cell's protein factories. The team used epigenetic engineering, changes to gene marks rather than gene code, on those genes.

Their title says this tuning enhances protein production. More active ribosomal genes mean more factories in each cell. Drug proteins are made in cultured mammalian cells, so higher yield cuts costs in a direct way. The route boosts output while the drug's own gene stays the same.
plos-pone-0006753:
Sayaka Wakayama and co-authors simulated weightlessness for early mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2009. Life beyond Earth will require mammal reproduction in space. How the space environment affects reproduction is poorly understood. Doing such experiments in real space is difficult. Most prior work used simpler animals or single cells.

The team grew mouse embryos before implantation under simulated microgravity. Development suffered detrimental effects in vitro. Early embryos are a key phase where damage has lasting consequences. Problems at this stage could block reproduction on stations or other planets. The results argue that gravity plays a quiet but real role in earliest development.
plos-pone-0006853:
Li Zhou and his team studied a gate that steers how cells ship out cholesterol in PLOS ONE in 2009. A carrier called ABCA1 moves cholesterol out to a blood protein. That move pulls the fatty stuff out of the body's far tissues. Too little of the carrier lets cholesterol pile up in cells. The gate here is a cell sensor called LRP1.

LRP1 steered two steps of the exit path. It set how much ABCA1 the cell made. It also set a tag placed on an enzyme in the path. One gate at both steps means tight joint control. The path counts for clogged arteries, where cholesterol builds in the walls. It gives drug work more than one place to step in.
plos-pone-0006953:
Akio Kuroda, Tibor Rauch, Ivan Todorov, and colleagues studied control of the insulin gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. Insulin is central to how the body manages fuel. Most switches that turn the insulin gene on had already been found. Far less was known about one chemical layer of control, DNA methylation.

The team showed that methylation of the gene's DNA helps regulate its expression. Methyl marks can quiet a gene without changing its code. Their finding adds an epigenetic dial to insulin control. That matters for diabetes research, since insulin output fails or falters in that disease.
plos-pone-0007053:
James Brody reconsidered how cancers develop in PLOS ONE in 2009. The classic multi-stage idea says cancers pass through one defined series of genetic changes. Age patterns in cancer data first suggested that idea over fifty years ago. Modern studies of tumor molecules, though, point to several different routes.

Brody re-examined the age-specific incidence data behind the classic model. He argued the data fit parallel routes of carcinoma development. Different roads to the same cancer change how risk should be calculated. They also affect screening, since each route may set its own pace.
plos-pone-0007153:
László Héja, Péter Barabás, Gabriella Nyitrai, and colleagues studied support cells in the brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. Glutamate and GABA are the brain's main go and stop signals. Glial transporters clear glutamate from the spaces between cells. GABA was thought to be cleared mainly by neurons. Astrocytes, the star-shaped glial cells, complicate that picture.

The team showed glutamate uptake can trigger GABA release from astrocytes. The release runs through a transporter working in reverse. In effect, a burst of activity makes support cells release a calming signal. That feedback may protect circuits from overexcitation.
plos-pone-0007253:
Christopher A. Sontag, Harvey Sage, and Harold P. Erickson studied bacterial building-block proteins in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Two tubulin-like genes, BtubA and BtubB, occur in the bacterium Prosthecobacter. Tubulins normally form the hollow tubes that shape eukaryotic cells and move chromosomes during division.

Crystal structures suggested BtubB matches alpha-tubulin and BtubA matches beta-tubulin. Equal mixtures of the two proteins assemble into tubulin-like protofilaments. The authors show the paired BtubA-BtubB heterodimer is an essential intermediate in that assembly. Their result helps explain how complex cell skeletons may have evolved from simpler bacterial parts.
plos-pone-0007353: Alan W. Meerow, Larry Noblick, James W. Borrone, and colleagues presented a phylogenetic analysis of plant genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject is a set of seven WRKY genes. WRKY genes encode transcription regulators found in plants, where they help control responses to stress and disease. The authors compare those genes across plant groups to trace their evolutionary relationships, using sequence differences to build a family history of the genes.
plos-pone-0007453:
Dale Webster and colleagues published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on measuring variation inside virus populations. A virus sample is rarely one genome repeated. It is a swarm of close variants. Older techniques could describe a few variants in detail or the whole swarm only roughly. The authors set out to get both detail and coverage.

They describe an enhanced single base extension technique that reads mutation frequencies at each position of the genome. That gives a fine-grained census of the whole population at once. Researchers can watch drug resistance or immune escape arise variant by variant. The method is a practical tool for anyone tracking how viruses evolve inside a host.
plos-pone-0007553:
Sing-Guan Kong and colleagues published a mathematical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on symmetry hidden inside genomes. The cause of a symmetry is often subtle, and studying one can reveal deeper truths about its bearer. The team conducted a broad survey of textual symmetries across hundreds of complete chromosomes. Their focus was inverse symmetry, a mirror-like property in DNA sequences, and the idea of whole-genome inverse duplication.

The patterns they found offer clues about how genomes grow and evolve. A genome that duplicates in reverse leaves a recognizable signature behind. Measuring that signature across many species shows how common the process has been. Genome architecture is not random; it carries the marks of its own history. The study reads those marks with statistics drawn from a very large sample.
plos-pone-0007653:
Dana Royer and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how red maple leaves change shape with climate. A leaf's form can reflect flexible response, called plasticity, or fixed genetic differences. Leaf teeth and the depth of leaf lobes are traits known to track temperature in fossils. How plastic those traits are was a critical gap. The team measured leaves across a temperature gradient to separate flexibility from inheritance.

Leaf shape showed real plasticity along the gradient. The same genetic stock can produce different leaves in different temperatures. That flexibility matters for predicting how trees respond as the climate warms. It also matters for reading fossil leaves: shape reflects both ancestry and the weather of a leaf's own lifetime. The study quantifies a response that paleobotanists use as a thermometer.
plos-pone-0007753:
Patricia Scolari Fontela and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It grades the quality of test-accuracy research on three diseases: TB, HIV and malaria. Studies that judge diagnostic tests are often weak in method and reporting. Two standards, QUADAS and STARD, were issued in 2003 to fix that.

The authors checked whether studies in these fields actually meet the standards. They scored both the methods used and how fully results were reported. Clear reporting lets clinicians trust a test's claimed accuracy. The review shows where diagnostic research still falls short.
plos-pone-0007853:
Samuel Shepard and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explores how animals splice out very large introns from their genes. Introns are the stretches cut from a gene's message before use. In mammals, most genes contain introns, and hundreds of them run past fifty thousand letters.

Splicing such huge introns out on time is a logistical feat. Distant ends of the message must be brought together accurately. The authors describe the peculiar ways large introns are handled. Their account helps explain splicing errors, which underlie some genetic diseases. It also refines models of how genes are read.
plos-pone-0007953:
Barbara Wegiel and colleagues studied a protein that brakes prostate cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, cystatin C, blocks a set of enzymes that chew through tissue. In healthy tissue those enzymes do useful work, but tumors can turn them loose to spread.

In prostate tumors the brake protein ran low. With less of it, cancer cells pushed into nearby tissue more freely, through paths that involve known growth signals. The work suggests restoring or copying the brake could slow spread, and that its loss may warn of a more pushy tumor.
plos-pone-0008053:
Greg Thurber and colleagues lit tumors in many colors to guide the surgeon's knife in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cutting a tumor out in full is among the best cancer cures, but small clusters hide against healthy tissue and get left behind. Those clusters seed relapse.

Using glowing tags of several colors and a live microscope, the team made cancer cells stand out during surgery in mice. Seeing the glow in real time let them cut more cleanly. The method is early, but it aims at one of surgery's oldest problems: what the eye cannot see, it cannot remove.
plos-pone-0008153:
Marco Salemi and colleagues traced how HIV changes inside the tumors of lymphoma patients in PLOS ONE in 2009. Even with strong modern therapy, people with HIV face far higher rates of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Macrophages, a kind of immune cell, shelter the virus and travel widely.

Virus taken from separate tumor sites had evolved in distinct directions, site by site. The virus was not one strain marching in step, but many local lines adapting where they sat. Care for HIV-linked cancers must reckon with that local variety, since a drug must work in every site.
plos-pone-0008253:
Jörg U. Ganzhorn and colleagues compared primate communities across continents in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Tropical primate groups differ strikingly between regions. The Americas have fewer leaf-eating but more fruit-eating genera than the Old World. Why these communities evolved so differently is poorly understood. Fruit protein content is one candidate explanation the team examined.

They weighed possible fruit protein effects in Madagascar and the Neotropics. If fruit quality differs by region, diets and community makeup could follow. Testing ecological factors like this helps explain primate evolution. The study links food chemistry to broad patterns in nature.
plos-pone-0008353:
Paula Irles, Xavier Bellés, and M. Dolors Piulachs studied an eggshell gene in insects in PLOS ONE in 2009. An insect eggshell must protect the yolk and embryo inside. It must also let air in for respiration and let sperm enter. Tiny structures called aeropyles and micropyles handle those jobs. Insects that lay eggs in a case face a double breathing problem.

The gene brownie helps build complex respiratory devices in the eggshell. Understanding its role shows how shells gain their fine structures. That knowledge connects genetics to the engineering of the egg. It may also inform pest control strategies.
plos-pone-0008453:
Adrian Ong and co-authors tackled flu diagnosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The new influenza A H1N1 virus of 2009 showed a broad range of signs. Signs also changed as it reached new places and groups. Doctors in clinics had to guess if a patient had flu. Wrong guesses waste tests and delay care.

The team compare cases of the new flu with other cases. They look for signs that predict infection with more accuracy. Their aim is a better rule for use in an outpatient setting. A sharper rule could guide testing and treatment in a pandemic surge.
plos-pone-0008553:
Manabu Igarashi and co-authors predict the shape of pandemic flu in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The 2009 H1N1 virus had just entered the human population. Its key surface gene came from a swine flu virus. That swine virus likely shares a root with the 1918 pandemic virus. The surface protein, called HA, is the main target of antibodies. Its outer sites decide if past immunity can spot a new strain.

The team model the shape of those outer sites. A good model helps predict how the virus may change over time. It also helps design shots that match future strains. Such work supports planning for a pandemic.
plos-pone-0008653:
Ji-Hyeon Lee and co-authors study beta cell renewal in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Insulin-producing beta cells are destroyed or impaired in diabetes. Replacing functional beta cell mass would advance diabetes care. Cdk4, a cell cycle kinase, was previously shown to be important in regulating beta cell growth. The team test how Cdk4 recruits new beta cells. Sources include quiescent beta cells and ductal epithelial progenitors in the pancreas.

They find Cdk4 regulates recruitment of both sources to reconstitute beta cell mass. Activating dormant cells and progenitors restores insulin capacity. That dual recruitment offers a strategy for regenerative diabetes therapy. It complements approaches based on transplantation alone.
plos-pone-0008753:
Michael Riedel, Olaf Goldbaum, Lisa Schwarz, and colleagues tested a drug that helps cells clear protein clumps. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, alpha-synuclein, piles up in nerve cells in Parkinson disease and related disorders. Clumped protein resists normal disposal routes. A compound called 17-AAG was known to stress cell defenses in useful ways.

Treated cells switched on autophagy, their self-eating cleanup system. Clumps inside the cell body then cleared away faster. Turning up that cleanup could protect neurons from toxic buildup. The work supports autophagy-boosting strategies for brain diseases.
plos-pone-0008853:
Yuriy Mishchenko proposed painting synapses in color codes to map brain wiring with light. His single-author methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mapping every connection in dense brain tissue is a huge challenge. The Brainbow system tags neurons with random mixes of glowing proteins. Mishchenko extends that idea down to individual synapses. Each synapse would carry a color mix naming its parent neuron pair.

Optical detection could then read wiring diagrams from the colors. Dense neuropil, normally a tangle to electron microscopes, becomes readable by light. The proposal offers a faster path to connectome maps. Experimental tests will decide how far the idea carries.
plos-pone-0008953:
Raimond Gordienko and co-authors pictured antifreeze proteins sitting on ice-like crystals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oil and gas pipelines can clog with hydrates, crystals that form when gas meets cold water. The usual fix, methanol, is toxic and used in huge amounts. Proteins that keep fish from freezing offer a greener possible substitute.

The team imaged the proteins where they meet the hydrate crystals. The pictures show how the proteins grip the crystal surface and block its growth. A blocker borrowed from nature could cut the chemicals the industry pumps into pipes. The study is an early step toward that cleaner kind of pipeline protection.
plos-pone-0009053:
Suzanne Angeli, Jieya Shao, and Marc Diamond studied two disease proteins that grab the cell's skeleton, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One is the androgen receptor; the other is huntingtin, of Huntington disease fame. Both diseases worsen when a glutamine stretch in the protein grows too long. Long stretches destabilise the proteins and drive them into clumps.

The team found regions on both proteins that bind F-actin, the skeleton's cables. Those grips increased how much the proteins clumped. They also changed the clumps' character once formed. Clinging to the skeleton may be part of how these proteins turn harmful.
plos-pone-0009153:
Jie Wen and co-authors checked European diabetes gene finds in a Han Chinese group, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genome-wide scans had tied several variants to type 2 diabetes. Most of those scans were run in people of European ancestry. Whether the same genes matter in East Asians needed testing.

The team genotyped risk alleles in a Han Chinese cohort. Three loci held up as genuine susceptibility genes: CDKN2A/B, CDKAL1, and TCF7L2. Other European hits did not confirm as clearly. Diabetes genetics clearly crosses ancestries, but not gene for gene.
plos-pone-0009253:
Guillaume Lucas and co-authors published this rat study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most antidepressants take weeks to work, a delay that can be dangerous. The team had earlier found that drugs acting on the serotonin 4 receptor act much faster. Here they asked whether combining the two kinds of drug could do even better.

They gave rats serotonin 4 receptor agonists together with standard antidepressants, the SSRIs used in clinics worldwide. The combination strengthened the rapid antidepressant-like effects in their tests. That result suggests a pairing strategy: a fast-acting drug boosted by a familiar one. Faster relief is a major unmet need in depression care.
plos-pone-0009353:
Camille Szmaragd and co-authors published this animal disease study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bluetongue is a virus spread by biting midges to sheep and cattle. It can sweep across huge distances in a season. In summer 2006, serotype 8 reached northern Europe for the first time and hit over two thousand farms.

The team modeled how the virus then spread through Great Britain. They also judged how well vaccination controlled it. A working model of spread lets officials aim vaccines and movement bans where they count. The study draws lessons from Britain's campaign for other countries facing the same virus.
plos-pone-0009453:
Martin Storr and colleagues studied a gene variant and bowel disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. The body has its own cannabis like signals. One receiver for those signals, called CNR1, helps calm the gut. The team looked at a common change in the CNR1 gene. They asked whether it alters the risk of bowel disease.

People with the variant had a changed risk of ulcerative colitis. The variant also shaped how Crohn's disease showed up in patients. Both diseases cause long term gut inflammation. The findings tie a single gene change to who gets sick and in what form. That could help explain why patients differ so much.
plos-pone-0009553:
Allan Dobbins and Jon Grossmann studied how people read three dimensional tilt in PLOS ONE in 2010. A wireframe cube can be seen in two ways. Most people first see it as if tilted down, viewed from above. That bias is strong in the first instant of looking. The team measured the bias across viewers and conditions.

Our visual system leans on learned facts about the world, such as light coming from above. Those habits shape what we see before thought can intervene. Measuring the bias tells us how strong those habits are. It helps explain why some optical illusions fool almost everyone at first glance.
plos-pone-0009653:
Francoise Bruyere and co-authors asked whether a clotting protein also builds lymph vessels in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein is PAI-1. Its known job is to slow the breakdown of blood clots. Lymph vessels drain fluid from tissues and carry immune cells. Their growth is called lymphangiogenesis. The team tested whether PAI-1 drives that growth.

Experiments in their model weighed the protein's effect on new lymph vessel formation. A familiar clotting factor moonlighting in vessel building would link two systems. The question matters for cancer, since tumors use lymph vessels to spread. It also matters for swelling disorders where drainage fails.
plos-pone-0009753:
Interferons are signal proteins the body releases to fight viruses. Simon Waddell and colleagues studied the gene programs interferons switch on in human blood cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

A transcriptional program is a coordinated set of genes turned on together. Dissecting those programs means separating their parts so each can be read clearly. The work used cells from human peripheral blood, the blood in general circulation. Clear maps of interferon programs help researchers read immune activity in many diseases. Each program is a fingerprint of a specific immune state.
plos-pone-0009853:
Genes can be turned up or down by chemical marks on the proteins that spool DNA. Dongqing Wang and colleagues mapped such marks on one gene's promoter. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The gene makes TSH-alpha, part of the thyroid-stimulating hormone. The marks sit on histones, the spool proteins DNA wraps around. Distinct, histone-specific modifications mediated positive versus negative regulation of the promoter. In plain terms, different marks pushed the gene opposite ways. The work shows how fine the control of one gene can be. Promoters are the on-switches that sit before a gene.
plos-pone-0009953:
A cytokine known for building immune cells also talks to the brain's appetite center. Laurence Macia and colleagues traced that new role in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cytokine is interleukin-7. The hypothalamus sits deep in the brain's base.

The target is the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, a brain hub for hunger signals. There, interleukin-7 played a part in regulating body weight and food intake. Immune signals reaching appetite circuits blur the line between defense and metabolism. The finding adds a player to obesity research. Appetite centers weigh many signals at once.
plos-pone-0010153:
The authors were Martín Ravetti, Osvaldo Rosso, Regina Berretta, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study searched for markers of decline in Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's steadily destroys cognition, measured in life by a standard mental state exam. After death, counts of neurofibrillary tangles help characterize the disease in the hippocampus, a memory region.

The team linked those decline measures to gene activity profiles in the hippocampus. Molecular markers that track with cognition could reveal disease steps in finer detail. Such markers might later help test drugs against specific stages of decline.
plos-pone-0010253:
Yun Wang, Amey Barakat, and Hongwei Zhou measured direct electrical links between brain cells in 2010. Electrical synapses, also called gap junctions, let neurons pass signals straight to each other. They help neurons fire in sync, which many brain functions and disorders depend on. Most past work focused on interneurons, a smaller class of brain cells.

Their PLOS ONE study examined direct electrical coupling among pyramidal cells of the neocortex. Pyramidal cells are the cortex's main output neurons, central to thought and perception. Evidence of direct coupling between them changes how cortical networks are modeled.
plos-pone-0010353:
Dinler Antunes, Gustavo Vieira, Maurício Rigo and colleagues modeled how the immune system displays protein pieces, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells show fragments of their inner proteins on surface holders called MHC class I. Killer immune cells scan those displays for signs of infection. Each holder type grips fragments in its own pattern. Predicting which fragments fit which holder is a key puzzle.

The team rebuilt holder-and-fragment structures on a computer. They looked for shape patterns that depend on the holder's gene version. Good models can flag which viral pieces the immune system is likely to notice. That helps vaccine design and studies of cross-reaction, where one display fools cells into attacking another. Shape, here, decides what the immune system sees.
plos-pone-0010453:
Odd Aksel Bergstad and colleagues studied what a deep-sea fish eats along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in PLOS ONE in 2010. The roundnose grenadier is among the most common large fish on that undersea mountain chain. Its feeding on continental slopes was fairly well known. The ridge habitat, far from land, could offer a different menu. The team examined stomach contents and related measures from ridge-caught fish.

Knowing what a dominant fish eats reveals how energy moves through deep ecosystems. The ridge hosts fisheries interest and unique species side by side. Diet data help judge how fishing might ripple through the food web. Deep-sea ecology still rests on few such basic surveys. This one adds a key predator's menu to the record.
plos-pone-0010553:
Jianjun Sun and R. John Collier showed that bonds in a cell receptor are required for the anthrax toxin pore to work in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anthrax toxin enters cells through surface receptors that anchor it tightly. The receptor helps the toxin assemble and slip inside as acidity changes. One receptor, called receptor 2, has sulfur bonds in its outer part. The team tested whether those bonds matter for the toxin's pore.

Without intact bonds, the receptor-bound pore failed to function. A pore that cannot open cannot deliver the toxin's harmful parts. That makes the bonds a possible weak point for antidotes. Anthrax remains a biodefense concern as well as a natural disease. Basic pore mechanics, as here, guide countermeasure design.
plos-pone-0010653:
Nick Tolimieri and Marti Anderson measured fish diversity in a new way off California, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Counting species alone treats a herring and a shark as equal gains. Taxonomic distinctness instead weighs how distantly related the species in a catch are.

The authors applied the measure to bottom-dwelling fishes of the California Current. Patterns differed from plain species counts, highlighting areas rich in evolutionary variety. A site with fewer species could still hold more distinct lineages. Managers protecting distinctness, not just numbers, are more likely to preserve the full range of ocean life.
plos-pone-0010753:
Payam Nahid and colleagues checked whether TB strain family skewed a drug trial's results, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycobacterium tuberculosis falls into distinct lineages around the world. Lineages differ in spread and possibly in how disease presents. Trials rarely report which lineage each patient carried.

The team typed strains from patients in a large treatment trial. Lineage was indeed unevenly spread among trial sites. It also tracked with some patient traits. Left uncounted, strain mix could make one site or arm of a trial look better for reasons unrelated to the drug. Future TB trials, the authors argue, should type strains as a matter of routine.
plos-pone-0010853:
Yusuke Shiozawa, Younghun Jung, Anne Ziegler and co-authors published this study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bleeding wakes up blood-forming stem cells to replace lost blood, and the same cells can also prompt bone building by releasing growth factors. What switches the stem cells on was unclear, so the team tested erythropoietin, the hormone that rises after blood loss.

They found the hormone activates signaling inside blood stem cells, leading them to release bone-building factors. It also acted directly on bone-forming cells in culture, and in living animals bone removal came first, followed by new bone growth driven by the hormone and the stem cell factors. Shiozawa and colleagues describe a tidy loop linking blood recovery with skeleton repair after injury.
plos-pone-0010953:
Kenneth Catania published this animal behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tentacled snake hunts fish underwater by trickery: it feints with its body, startling the fish into fleeing straight toward its jaws. When a fish sits at a right angle, though, its escape dart carries it sideways, so the snake must strike where the fish will be, not where it is.

Catania tested laboratory-born snakes that had never hunted, filming strikes at hundreds of frames per second through a glass barrier that prevented any learning from success or failure. The naive snakes aimed at the fish's future position just as experienced adults do. Catania concludes the prediction is built in at birth, not learned. The study is a clean demonstration that a complex hunting forecast can be hardwired into a newborn brain.
plos-pone-0011053:
Clare Kirkpatrick, Piero Marchetti, Francesco Purrello and co-authors published this diabetes genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genome-wide studies had named several genes that raise type 2 diabetes risk, most assumed to act in insulin-making beta cells. The authors sorted human pancreatic islet cells into insulin-producing beta cells and glucagon-producing alpha cells to check where five risk genes actually speak.

All five genes, including FTO and TCF7L2, were expressed in both cell types rather than being beta-cell specific. Their levels were then compared against the age and body mass of the islet donors and between diabetic and non-diabetic tissue. Kirkpatrick and colleagues widen the cast of cells through which diabetes genes may act. Ignoring alpha cells could mean missing half the mechanism of inherited diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0011153:
Apicella, Cesarini, Johannesson and colleagues tested a popular hormone claim in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oxytocin is often called a love or trust hormone. The team asked whether gene variants in its receptor track with how generous or trusting people act in lab games.

They found no link between those gene variants and the social choices people made in the tests. Publishing a clear null result matters in a field prone to hype. It cautions against simple gene to behavior stories for complex social traits. Later claims about this hormone now have a firmer result to answer to.
plos-pone-0011253:
Ganguly, Basu, Chakraborty and colleagues attacked drug resistant cancer in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some tumors survive standard drugs by refusing to die on cue. The team used a newly developed iron binding compound aimed at the cell death pathway housed in mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

Triggering death through that route overcame resistance in their tests. Hitting the power plant sidesteps defenses that block other drugs at the cell surface. The approach offers a treatment plan for tumors that have exhausted common options. Further work must show the compound is safe in healthy tissue as well.
plos-pone-0011353:
Sung-Hun Lee and colleagues studied mouse jumping genes in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. L1 elements are stretches of DNA that can copy themselves and land in new spots in the genome. Near many of them sit CpG islands, short regions rich in two DNA letters that often mark where genes switch on.

The team asked whether those islands decide when an L1 element becomes active and starts to be read. Their results link the islands to the on-off control of these mobile elements. That control matters because active jumping genes can disrupt normal genes and reshape the genome over time. Knowing what wakes them helps geneticists judge the risk they pose and understand how genomes stay mostly stable despite carrying so many mobile parts.
plos-pone-0011453:
Heidi Schreiber and co-authors reported in 2010 that guard cells inside tuberculosis-like granulomas can hold back the very defense they should support. Granulomas are dense balls of immune cells that wall off mycobacteria in the lung. Dendritic cells inside them are expected to rally T cells against the trapped germs, and the team tested that expectation in mice.

Instead, dendritic cells in chronic granulomas restrained the local antibacterial T-cell response. The fortress metaphor thus flips: cells meant to organize the attack were damping it, which may help explain why these infections linger for years despite a strong immune presence. The finding matters for tuberculosis treatment and vaccine design. If the local brake can be released safely, the immune system might finish a job it currently leaves half done.
plos-pone-0011553:
Wanlop Jaidee, David Moher, and Malinee Laopaiboon measured in 2010 how fast the evidence base for pregnancy care goes stale. Cochrane reviews gather all trial evidence on a question and guide childbirth practice worldwide, but new trials keep arriving. The team studied the pregnancy and childbirth review collection, timing how long each review takes to need updating and how much its conclusions move when updated.

Reviews aged at different rates, and updating changed some results by amounts large enough to matter for practice. An audit of this kind tells guideline writers where to spend scarce updating effort first: on the reviews whose answers are both old and unstable. It also warns clinicians that a trusted review carries an expiry date. Good evidence is a living thing, and this study measures its lifespan.
plos-pone-0011653:
Bernhard Knapp and co-authors connected computer simulations to real immune responses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. T cells start an immune response when they recognise a peptide held by an MHC molecule. Slightly altered peptides can strengthen or weaken that response, but how the physical fit drives the outcome is not fully understood.

The team simulated the motion of altered peptides bound to MHC and compared the films with responses measured in living systems. Patterns in the simulations matched the strength of real responses. That screen-to-bench link helps researchers design altered peptides that tune immunity on purpose, for vaccines or therapy.
plos-pone-0011753:
John Cussans and co-authors compared pollination success in gardens versus farmland, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bee numbers run high where flowers are abundant, whether in mass-flowering crops or in densely planted gardens. Land management therefore shapes how much pollination wild plants receive.

The team found two bee-pollinated plant species produced much more seed when grown in gardens than on arable farmland. The garden advantage measures what intensive farming costs pollination in the wider landscape. It also suggests gardens act as refuges that support bees and the plants depending on them.
plos-pone-0011853:
Hui Zeng and colleagues described in 2010 how to steer human induced pluripotent stem cells into specific kinds of neurons. A general neuron is not enough for most uses; brain regions need their own cell types. The team focused on guiding the stem cells toward region-specific neurons, including the glutamate-using neurons of the forebrain.

Their work analyzes the steps that push flexible stem cells toward one regional identity rather than another. Reliable recipes of this sort are what labs need to grow brain tissue models in a dish. With the right cell types, researchers can study disorders of particular brain regions and test drugs on human cells instead of guessing from animal tissue.
plos-pone-0011953:
Ramsey Saleem and colleagues ran in 2010 a genome-wide hunt for genes that build and maintain peroxisomes. Peroxisomes are small compartments that handle tasks such as breaking down fatty acids, and cells make more of them when fatty signals call. The controls behind that building program are spread across many genes.

Screening the whole genome for effectors of peroxisome biogenesis produced a wide parts list, including genes not previously tied to these organelles. A fuller parts list helps explain diseases in which peroxisomes fail, such as those that damage the developing brain. It also shows how a cell coordinates construction of a whole compartment on demand.
plos-pone-0012053:
Jana Petermann and co-workers used a grassland experiment in 2010 to trace how losing plant species reaches insects two levels up the food chain. Biodiversity loss is usually measured on the plants themselves; effects on the life histories of higher trophic levels had barely been studied. Their subjects were aphids and the parasitoid wasps that attack them.

Measuring life-history traits across plant diversity levels showed that plant species loss changes how aphids live and how their parasitoids fare. A parasitoid is a natural pest controller, so its decline matters beyond ecology. The study shows biodiversity is load-bearing: remove plant species and the effects arrive, delayed, at the top of the chain.
plos-pone-0012153:
Wenyu Bu, Kim Buay Lim, Yuan Hong Yu, and co-authors studied how cells pull material inside, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The process starts with the cell membrane bending inward, guided by scaffold proteins and strands of actin, the cell's internal rope. Three partner proteins sit at the center of that bending work, and the team probed how their interactions shape the membrane.

They found the partners together drive the membrane into tubes, form small cargo bubbles, and move those bubbles along. This is the cell's import system at its most basic level. Understanding it helps explain how cells take in nutrients and signals, and how viruses and drugs find their way inside.
plos-pone-0012253:
Carsten Friis, Trudy Wassenaar, Muhammad Javed, and co-authors sequenced the genome of a Campylobacter strain with a known story, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Strain M1 is a rare documented case of this food-poisoning bacterium passing directly from a chicken to a person, causing gut illness. Having both the strain and its history makes its genome a reference point for tracing other infections.

They compared its full genome with a dozen other sequenced strains of the same species. Knowing how a proven chicken-to-human strain differs from harmless relatives can reveal the genes that make the jump between species possible. Food safety tracing depends on exactly such reference genomes when outbreaks need a source.
plos-pone-0012353:
Bader Al-Anzi and Kai Zinn warned fellow fly researchers in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper that a common fat test misleads. The fruit fly has become a key model for studying how genes control fat storage. Labs often measure stored fat, in the form of triglycerides, with a simple color test and assume the reading equals body fat.

Al-Anzi and Zinn show that the color test also picks up other fats, so its numbers cannot give a true measure of stored fat alone. Studies that trusted the test may have drawn wrong conclusions about which genes make flies fat or thin. Their caution pushes the field toward cleaner methods before strong claims are made.
plos-pone-0012453:
Bethany Hannas, Parikshit Das, Hong Li and colleagues exposed water fleas to nitrate pollution, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Nitrate and nitrite wash off farms into ponds everywhere, and water animals meet them often. The team found the harm is not just from contact: the crustacean Daphnia magna converts these chemicals inside its body into nitric oxide, a reactive gas.

That internal conversion harmed development of the young water fleas. Pollution limits set by testing chemicals in water alone may miss damage done after uptake and conversion. Daphnia are standard test animals for water safety, so the finding argues for closer looks at other farm chemicals too.
plos-pone-0012553:
Christopher Noto and Ari Grossman charted the ecology of Late Jurassic dinosaurs across whole continents, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Dinosaur distribution maps existed, but those data had rarely been turned to ecological questions — which climates and landscapes each group favored, and how communities were structured at broad scale. The Jurassic was the age of the giant long-necked sauropods.

Applying ecological analysis to the occurrence data, the authors drew out broad patterns in habitat use among dinosaur groups. Scale matters: patterns visible across continents can vanish in single quarries. Their approach shows paleontology can borrow the tools of modern ecology to read ancient ecosystems.
plos-pone-0012653:
Corbo, Ritelli, Barbi and co-authors hunted for cancer genes in pancreatic tumours by screening kinases. Kinases are proteins that switch other proteins on and off, and they often go wrong in cancer. Their 2010 study profiled kinase mutations in tumours of the pancreas duct and of the ampulla of Vater nearby.

Fresh mutations turned up candidate genes that may drive these hard-to-treat cancers. Pancreatic cancer still has very few good drug targets, so each solid candidate counts. The screen gives follow-up labs a short list to test in cells and patients.
plos-pone-0012753:
Benardais, Kasem, Couegnas and co-authors showed that mice lacking a stabilising protein grow fewer new smell neurons. The protein, called STOP, steadies the cell's internal rails, and mice without it show behaviour faults and weaker brain connections. Smell tissue is unusual because it rebuilds its neurons throughout life, making it a window on nerve growth.

Their 2010 study found that this rebuilding falters in the nose when STOP is missing. The mice also had smaller pools of the vesicles neurons use to send signals. The result ties a rail-steadying protein to the birth of new neurons, a link that may extend to brain repair research.
plos-pone-0336553:
Floor A van den Brand and three colleagues published a public health planning study in PLOS ONE in 2026. Paying workers to quit smoking can work, but a workplace program fails if it is built poorly. The team set out to design the rollout of such a program with care, using a formal method called Implementation Mapping.

Van den Brand's group worked through the method step by step, naming who must act, what has to change, and which supports are needed. The result is a detailed plan an employer can follow rather than a vague hope. For health promoters, the study shows how to turn proof that incentives work into a program that survives contact with a real workplace.
plos-pone-0339253:
Katharine Sykes and four colleagues validate an artificial intelligence tool for reading dog chest X-rays. Their 2026 study concerns two measurements vets take from radiographs. One estimates overall heart size, the other the size of the left atrium. Human measurers vary noticeably, both between observers and within repeats. The software, called MetronMind, promises consistency and speed. The study used over one thousand client-owned dogs of eighty breeds.

Two manual measuring methods were compared first. They agreed almost perfectly, with negligible bias between them. The software's readings were then benchmarked against a trained observer's. Statistical checks included correlation and agreement plots across right and left side images. Dogs varied widely in heart size, chest shape, and image quality, which makes the test realistic. Reliable automated measurement could standardise heart screening in busy clinics and flag enlargement earlier.
plos-pone-0339753:
June Labbancz and co-authors let green peach aphids loose on tomato plants fed with conventional or organic fertiliser, then watched the harvest and listened to the plants' genes. Aphids drain billions from greenhouse crops yearly, and organic growing is booming without much knowledge of how organically fed plants handle attack. Gene activity was tracked in leaves and fruit partway through the plants' lives.

Conventionally fed plants attracted heavier infestation, yet neither group lost yield or fruit quality, likely thanks to generous water and nutrients. Inside the leaves, both groups shifted their gene activity from building to breaking down, while fruit barely stirred; a stress hormone led the response. One gene network tied uniquely to the organic-plus-aphid combination, and the authors flag its hub gene for future crop improvement work.
plos-pone-0341253:
Hongbo Yu proposed a way to keep wireless data private when the radio channel itself keeps changing, which makes security keys go stale. Moving devices and bouncing signals mean channels shift faster than keys are usually refreshed, leaving gaps for eavesdroppers. The method mixes two chaotic number generators, patterns that look random yet can be rebuilt by the receiver, to widen the key space.

A learning network that reads key-use records predicts the right moment to refresh keys and triggers a fresh key when something looks off. The new key then feeds a standard cipher for the actual scrambling. The design aims at a moving target problem in mobile networks: protection that renews itself at the channel's pace, so privacy does not depend on yesterday's key still fitting today's airwaves.
plos-pone-0342353:
Eleanor Turnbull-Jones and co-authors recorded more than five hundred antibiotic sales across twenty-two community pharmacies in Kakamega County, western Kenya, during August twenty twenty-five. Kenya's rules require prescriptions for these drugs, yet nobody had documented what actually happens at rural counters outside the capital. Staff logged whether each sale had a prescription, what illness it targeted, and whether customers had taken antibiotics recently.

Nearly half the sales went ahead without any prescription. Chest infections, both upper and lower, drove most demand, and a familiar trio of antibiotics dominated. Some customers received partial courses, usually because money ran short, a practice that breeds drug resistance. The authors identify plain stewardship gaps and argue that pharmacy-level rules and support, not just hospital programmes, are essential in the fight against resistant germs.
plos-pone-0342953:
Mohammed Tawfik and co-workers build a speech emotion reader that learns across separate sites without pooling raw recordings. Emotion tools trained on one collection usually stumble on another, and voices are private data. Their 2026 system trains five sites in two languages together under formal privacy guarantees, fusing a pattern-reading network with an attention network to judge feelings from voice.

Scores on familiar test sets ran near perfect. On a completely new collection, accuracy fell to about two-thirds, with lively emotions transferring better than quiet ones. Feature pruning and the privacy method each contributed gains in step-by-step checks. The drop on new data shows cross-culture emotion reading remains genuinely hard, privacy or not.
plos-pone-0343753:
Deogratius Kinoko and six colleagues analyze HIV testing patterns among Tanzanian girls and young women in this 2026 PLOS One study, a group at high risk of infection. The authors drew on two national surveys, from 2016/17 and 2022/23, covering more than twelve thousand respondents aged fifteen to twenty-four. They compared testing rates between teenagers and young adults and looked for factors tied to getting tested.

Testing among adolescents stayed flat at about two in five across both surveys, while among young women it rose to nine in ten. Being in a relationship, having more schooling, and having had a sexually transmitted infection were each tied to higher testing in both age groups. The authors argue for interventions aimed squarely at adolescents, alongside integrated reproductive and HIV services.
plos-pone-0344153:
Denis Mongin, Johan N Siebert, and co-authors asked why some Geneva neighborhoods send far more children to the pediatric emergency department for minor problems. Crowded departments and low-urgency visits often signal gaps in everyday care. Their 2026 study gathered all visits by children up to age sixteen across two years, grouping them by neighborhood and urgency level.

About half of the nearly sixty-eight thousand visits were low urgency. Two forces worked independently: living closer to the hospital raised use, and so did neighborhood social and economic vulnerability, each explaining up to about a fifth of minor visits. Having more pediatricians nearby helped only slightly. The authors warn that simply expanding primary care would miss these drivers, and they suggest outreach near hospitals and stronger health literacy support for families.
plos-pone-0344453:
Cruz-Jiménez and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how a smoker's social circle shapes whether they talk about quitting. Conversations sparked by anti-smoking messages often precede quit attempts, yet who starts them was little studied. About three hundred seventy American adults who smoke received cigarettes in packs carrying new warning labels and inserts about quitting, and reported nightly for two weeks.

Each day, the chance of talking about smoking's harms or quitting's benefits was tied to the makeup of the person's circle. Having contacts who disapproved of smoking raised the odds of harm talk. Curiously, having more smokers in the circle also raised talk, giving more occasions to discuss it. The authors map these egocentric networks, meaning the web seen from one person's chair, to show that messages do not land on isolated smokers; they land in conversations waiting to happen.
plos-pone-0345553:
Dasom Lee and colleagues worked with seven hundred fifty-three Korean employees whose jobs demand heavy emotional control, such as smiling through difficult encounters with the public. Their 2026 observational study split workers into high and low intensity groups, compared their mental health, and then offered everyone a single thirty-five minute mind-body training session.

Feeling emotionally out of tune with the job, and getting hurt by it, went with worse mood and lower quality of life in both groups. Workers who lacked support from their organisation fared worst. After the brief training, the high intensity group showed the biggest drop in negative feelings. The authors suggest workplaces should weigh emotional demands when planning support.
plos-pone-0347453:
Feng Gao and four colleagues published this 2026 simulation study of spray calcination, a process that turns high-level liquid nuclear waste into a stable solid. Incomplete reactions and solid buildup plague the equipment. Their three-dimensional model burned a nitric acid, sugar, and nitrate mixture while varying wall heat, packing porosity, flow speed, and ingredient strengths.

Hotter walls steadily raised the desired oxide product, and sugar proved the strongest lever on yield, beating equal boosts of the other ingredients. A gentle inflow speed worked best. Gao's settings aim at fuller reaction and better solid recovery.
plos-pone-0347753:
Gerry Hughes and co-workers survey hospital staff about joining research as their hospital works toward becoming an academic health science centre. Hospitals that fold research into daily care often see better patient results. Their 2026 study sends a short survey through wards and offices and gathers six hundred forty replies, mixing scored questions with open comments.

Most staff valued research and many had already taken part in some. The biggest blocks were lack of time, thin support, and scarce resources. Over half wanted more research training. Protected time, help with statistics, and simpler approvals topped the wish list. The results give hospital leaders a shopping list for turning goodwill into real studies.
plos-pone-0348053:
Lacey Boltz and colleagues grouped nearly a thousand British and Irish butterflies and moths by shared traits, asking whether extinction risk follows whole ways of life rather than single features. Species were linked into a similarity network based on their life cycles, timing, and development, and natural clusters were allowed to emerge without any knowledge of which species are threatened.

Nine strategy groups appeared, organised mainly by season timing and life-cycle pattern. Threatened species were far from evenly spread. One group, species producing several generations a year and developing out in the open, carried about six times the expected share of threatened species in both Britain and Ireland. The authors argue that conservation triage for poorly monitored insects should target risky strategies, not only named species.
plos-pone-0348353:
Fahad Rahman and co-authors proposed a blockchain based multi factor login system in 2026. Passwords plus codes are standard protection, yet central login servers are single points of failure and tempting targets.

Their design spreads authentication records across a blockchain network, removing the central vault and using the chain's tamper proofing to guard integrity. Login data stays available through outages, and privacy rests on shared agreement rather than one keeper. The authors report better load handling for busy services than older methods. The concept paper maps architecture and uses rather than reporting a live deployment.
plos-pone-0348953:
Mouna Stayoussef and colleagues searched the blood of breast cancer patients for immune checkpoint proteins that could flag the disease early. These proteins are the brakes and accelerators of anti-tumor immunity, and some float freely in serum. Using a multiplex test that reads sixteen at once, they compared eighty-eight untreated patients with forty-nine healthy controls.

Seven proteins differed clearly between the groups, and together they identified cancer with accuracy beating the two standard blood markers, while a distinct eight-protein pattern marked the aggressive triple-negative subtype. The panel also related to chemotherapy response and early progression. A blood test that both detects breast cancer and sorts its hardest subtype could spare patients invasive steps and speed treatment choices.
plos-pone-0349153:
Ikenna Onoh and colleagues described a trial plan in 2026 for finding and cutting lead exposure in young children in Nairobi, Kenya. Lead harms growing brains, and cities in poorer countries rarely run screening programs. No results are reported yet.

First, the team will adapt screening tools with local partners and pilot blood lead checks plus parent advice in an existing mother and child group. Then a clinic trial will screen about fifteen hundred children. Those with raised levels will get either clinic advice alone or added home focused support. The design tests both whether children benefit and whether clinics can sustain the program.
plos-pone-0349553:
Suzanne Schuh and co-authors published a trial plan in 2026 for magnesium given by vein to children with bad asthma attacks in emergency departments. Guidelines suggest it for severe cases, but proof is shaky and the treatment can lower blood pressure. No results are reported yet.

Six Canadian children's hospitals will enrol children aged two to seventeen who stay in clear distress after standard first treatment. They will get magnesium or a salt water dummy, and breathing scores two hours later form the main test. A firm answer could either spare children an intense therapy or confirm its early place.
plos-pone-0349753:
Hung Tran-Nam and Ha Che-Ngoc propose a clustering method for data that are uncertain and lopsided, where small groups drown inside big ones. Many records are better described as spread out probability curves than as single points. Their method pairs a bird inspired search, named for the black winged kite, with fuzzy grouping that uses a distance built for comparing curves.

On synthetic curves, skewed spreads, and real image data, the method beat four rival groupers and reached near perfect agreement with true groups where rivals scored near zero. Smarter starting points and curve aware distance drove the gains. Banks, hospitals, and image analysts facing rare but vital groups could benefit.
plos-pone-0349853:
Jialun Chen and Xixin Yan led a study of lung blood clots in rabbits over two weeks. They tracked two harmful processes. One is the web-like traps that immune cells throw out.
