The other is a form of cell death driven by iron. Gene scans and blood tests showed both at work. Trap levels peaked at day seven.

The team then tested a clot drug with and without an added enzyme. The enzyme breaks down the immune traps. The pair beat the drug alone on scar growth, oxygen levels, and heart strain. A side test group backed the trap pathway. The authors say drugs that clear traps may boost clot care.
plos-pone-0349953:
Enrico Fiore, Anastasia Lisuzzo, and co-authors used lung ultrasound to judge how well different vaccination plans protect dairy calves from respiratory disease, a major cost in cattle farming. Their 2026 study enrolled one hundred forty-nine calves, sorted by whether their lungs were healthy or already diseased at the start, and by vaccine plan: none, nose-spray only, or nose-spray plus injection.

Ultrasound scores and lesion areas grew over time in unvaccinated calves, healthy or not. The spray alone held lesion growth steady in healthy calves and shrank damaged areas in sick ones. The combined plan performed best overall, preserving healthy lungs and reducing consolidation in diseased calves. The authors conclude that pairing both vaccine routes best slows lung damage, and that ultrasound tracks the benefit without invasive tests.
plos-pone-0350453:
Kauzner and colleagues set out a study plan in 2026 on links between self-help groups and hospice care in Germany. People with life-limiting illness and their caregivers often find strength in groups of peers facing the same situation. Yet how such groups handle death and grief, and how they connect with professional hospice services, is barely studied.

Interviews with patients, caregivers, and staff from both worlds will run through mid-2027. The team will turn findings into tailored recommendations for each group of actors. Better links could help families find peer support earlier, rather than discovering groups only by chance near the end of life.
plos-pone-0350553:
Heba Mohammed Arafat and co-authors studied growth factor blood levels and a gene variant in Palestinian women with breast cancer in 2026. The proteins involved help control cell growth, and their links to hormone receptor types may refine risk reading.

One hundred twelve newly diagnosed patients gave interviews, blood, and tumor tissue results. Most tumors were positive for estrogen and progesterone receptors, and most lacked the HER2 marker. The gene variant tied significantly to progesterone receptor status and to combined receptor positivity. Studies from underrepresented populations matter: risk markers found elsewhere do not always behave the same in Palestinian patients.
plos-pone-0350653:
Demet Yalçın Kehribar and co-authors tested the lung drug roflumilast against sepsis like injury in rats in 2026. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, damages many organs, and a bacterial toxin is a standard way to model it in animals.

Rats given the toxin showed high inflammation markers and harm to liver, kidney, and other tissues. A lower drug dose did nothing clear, but the higher dose cut inflammation signals, eased tissue damage, and lowered a kidney injury marker. The dose contrast is the story: protection appeared only at the stronger dose, a caution for any move toward patients.
plos-pone-0351053:
Zhao and colleagues studied how two neuron types help monkeys adapt to a brain-controlled cursor in a 2026 paper. Two monkeys steered the device while researchers varied how hard the control mapping changed. Neurons were sorted by signal shape into likely excitatory and likely inhibitory kinds.

Inhibitory-type neurons fired more and joined the learning process more strongly than excitatory ones. Task difficulty changed how both groups responded and coordinated. The results challenge the habit of treating all neurons alike in brain-device design. Tuning decoders to the special role of fast inhibitory cells could make prosthetic control adapt faster for users.
plos-pone-0351153:
Zhu, Liu, and Yang improved control of a motion-compensated gangway in a 2026 study. Such gangways bridge ships and offshore platforms, adjusting constantly as waves roll the vessel. Ship motion is erratic and the hydraulics behave nonlinearly, which strains standard controllers.

Their improved layered controller adds compensation for motion in several directions at once, based on a full dynamic model of the gangway. Simulations tested the design against ship movement. Steadier gangways mean safer crew transfers to wind farms and platforms, where a lurching bridge can injure workers. Better control also widens the weather window in which transfers can proceed.
plos-pone-0351553:
Yao-Hsiang Chen and colleagues tested a simple breathing trainer for people left breathless by COVID-19. The device is an incentive spirometer. Patients draw deep breaths against it to retrain the lungs. The trial ran at a hospital in northern Taiwan. Eighty-five patients took part after recovery. They were grouped by time since infection, from under three months to a year. Training ran three times a week for six weeks. A waiting group served as the control.

The waiting group did not improve. Breathlessness and daily function stayed flat. Every training group improved on both measures. That held even a full year after infection. A cheap plastic device plus coached practice moved symptoms that had stuck for months.
plos-pone-0351653:
Varun C. M and co-authors tackle a housekeeping problem inside cloud computing: spreading work evenly across virtual machines as demand keeps changing. Poor spreading leaves some machines overloaded and others idle, which slows answers and wastes resources. Their method borrows from the way Harris hawks hunt together, adjusting their positions as a group closes in on prey.

The algorithm searches for task placements that score well on several goals at once, including fast response and efficient use of machines. In the team's tests it beat other load-balancing methods on response time and resource use. Because conditions in real data centers shift minute by minute, a method that rebalances on the fly could help cloud services stay fast without extra hardware.
plos-pone-0351753:
Hossam Eldin Elgendy and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study of why psychiatric patients return to emergency departments within a year of leaving hospital in Alberta, Canada. The analysis followed more than a thousand people discharged from acute psychiatric units, using data from a transitional care study. The team tested whether satisfaction with hospital care, text-message support, or peer support predicted later emergency visits.

The strongest predictor was simply having visited a psychiatric emergency department in the six months before admission. Unemployment and unstable housing also raised the likelihood of a return visit. Satisfaction with inpatient care and the support programs showed no independent link. The authors say preventing repeat crises depends less on the hospital stay itself and more on work, housing, and earlier patterns of emergency use.
plos-pone-0351853:
Jinlong Huang and colleagues priced a second-line treatment for pancreatic cancer in China. The regimen adds liposomal irinotecan to standard chemotherapy. The comparison was the same chemotherapy with a placebo. Pancreatic cancer leaves patients few options, and this drug is costly. The team built a lifetime cost model from the trial behind the regimen. It counted costs and quality-adjusted years of life.

The drug bought a small slice of healthy time, about one quality-adjusted month. Its cost per unit of gain sat far beyond China's usual limit. No fair change in the inputs rescued the result. Only a price cut of nearly ninety percent would make it good value. The study hands negotiators a hard number to argue from.
plos-pone-0351953:
Huimin Lu and colleagues built a neural network to outline brain tumors in three-dimensional MRI scans. Surgeons and radiation teams plan from such maps. The tumor here is glioma, and glioblastoma is its most deadly form. Their model mixes two network styles. It adds a gate that focuses attention where tumors are likely to sit. A second part polishes each tumor region layer by layer. A special scoring rule punishes fuzzy borders.

On two public benchmark sets, the model scored near the top of current methods. It also cut border errors sharply. Border errors are the ones that matter most when a cut or a beam edge is planned. The outlines can also feed standard clinical scoring of tumor features.
plos-pone-0352253:
Alaina Beauchamp and co-authors mapped drug-resistant gut bacteria against an environmental justice index in an American urban county. Carbapenem-resistant organisms threaten hospitals worldwide, and the environment's role in their spread is understudied. Their 2026 study used health records from two large systems across six years and tested for spatial clustering by census tract.

The justice index itself clustered strongly across the county. Tracts scoring worse on the index showed higher local rates of resistant infections. The health vulnerability part of the index, capturing chronic disease burden, linked most strongly of all. Built environment measures also contributed. Beauchamp and colleagues argue resistance control should look beyond hospital walls to neighbourhood conditions.
plos-pone-0352353:
Swathi and Rajalakshmi combined two AI methods to find and sort brain tumors in scan images in a 2026 study. Tumor scans vary widely and labeled examples are few, which limits standard training. One method invents extra realistic scan images, while the other searches for the best network shape on its own.

Joining the two raised both outlining and sorting accuracy while keeping computing costs down, the authors report. Extra invented images eased the shortage of training data. The search method also cut the time needed to test network shapes by building them more cleverly. The authors present the pairing as a practical path toward faster scan reading in clinics, pending real-world trials.
plos-pone-0352453:
Nancy Cocunubo-Cocunubo and co-authors review in 2026 hospital isolates of a pneumonia causing bacterium in Meta, Colombia, for a trait that lets it resist many common antibiotics. Thousands of isolates not already resistant to the strongest drug class were drawn from routine surveillance over five years. Links with patient, sample, and hospital traits were tested in layered models.

About one in four isolates showed the resistance trait, and its share rose over time. Male sex, being an inpatient, and urine samples linked independently to the trait, with clear differences between hospitals. The authors urge stronger watching and tighter control of antibiotic use, since the pattern reflects care settings as much as biology.
plos-pone-0352753:
Guangwen Zhu and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One computational study on why people with type 2 diabetes lose muscle, a combination that worsens health in older adults. Oxidative stress is suspected to link the two conditions. Combining single-cell and bulk gene data from public datasets, the team used machine learning across many algorithm pairings to find the genes most central to the overlap.

Seven hub genes emerged, forming a connected set centered on inflammation signaling and the cell's protein-disposal machinery, which when overactive breaks down muscle. The genes also separated patients from controls accurately in several datasets. The authors propose them as candidate markers and drug targets, while noting the findings come from data analysis and need laboratory confirmation.
plos-pone-0352853:
Valentina Moccia and seven colleagues report a 2026 proof-of-concept study on whale and dolphin breath. When these animals surface, they exhale a spray called blow. That spray can be collected without capturing or harming the animal. The team asked whether blow carries extracellular vesicles, tiny parcels shed by cells that reveal health information.

Samples came from five bottlenose dolphins in human care and one wild long-finned pilot whale. Two purification methods were compared, and the particles were checked by size tracking, microscopy, and protein tests. Both species' blow contained vesicle-like particles of the expected size. Standard vesicle marker proteins were present as well. The result opens a gentle new route for monitoring health in wild cetaceans.
plos-pone-0353153:
ZhaoLiang Zhu and Xin Huang published this 2026 engineering simulation of buried pipelines crossing earthquake faults that slide sideways. Their pipe combines a steel wire frame with polyethylene plastic. A detailed three-dimensional model tested crossing angles, wire thickness, and soil types to see how the pipe bends, buckles, and finally distorts.

Damage unfolded in three stages, from elastic bending to buckling to global collapse, and a crossing angle near one hundred and fifty degrees proved most dangerous. Loess soil gripped the pipe best. Zhu finds standard design codes ignore the angle effect and need rethinking.
plos-pone-0353353:
Jack Wippell and Laura Dugan examine in 2026 whether political leaders who endorse white replacement claims stir public attention and extremist action in the United States. They built a new dataset joining lawmaker endorsements that drew media coverage with search trends and measures of white supremacist activity and propaganda. Time based models then traced what followed endorsements at national and state level.

As endorsements piled up, white supremacist activity rose afterward in both national and state checks. Links to public attention on immigration were clearer within states than nationally, suggesting influence stays close to a lawmaker's own area. The authors frame elite speech as able to create a hostile climate around demographic change.
plos-pone-0353453:
Sharon Jalene and five colleagues published this 2026 survey study of recovery after a mass casualty event on a university campus. Students and staff rated their depression and anxiety from before the event and again months after, alongside belonging, perceived discrimination, fitness estimates, and what kind of help they wanted.

Reported symptoms rose after the event, worst among students who felt they belonged least. Many respondents preferred learning exercise or meditation over visiting campus counseling. Jalene argues recovery planning should build belonging and offer varied routes to help, not a single doorway.
plos-pone-0353653:
Xiaolan Meng and seven colleagues study a compound gut bacteria make. It is called sodium butyrate. Their work shows it can push liver cancer cells into two kinds of death at once. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The team worked in cell cultures and in tumour-bearing animals. They traced the compound's attack step by step. It lowered a stress-response protein and its partner transporter. That let iron-driven damage, called ferroptosis, build up.

The damage wrecked the cells' power stations. That then triggered apoptosis, the classic self-destruct programme. A drug that blocks ferroptosis protected the tumours in animals. This confirmed the pathway's role. Since butyrate is a natural gut product, a gentler medicine may follow. It would be built on the body's own chemistry.
plos-pone-0353753:
Huijuan Bi and three colleagues build a blood test model to catch stomach and bowel tumors early, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Gastrointestinal tumors are usually found late, and single blood markers miss too much. The team compared two hundred fourteen patients with one hundred thirty tumor free controls across thirty-eight routine laboratory measures. They distilled seven core variables. Then they trained eleven machine learning algorithms to separate the groups.

One marker, serum cystatin 4, already stood higher in patients, though weak alone. The support vector machine model won the contest, scoring well on overall discrimination and catching over ninety-five percent of tumors, at the price of more false alarms among the healthy. An explanation analysis credited blood count, the cystatin marker, and age as the strongest inputs. The authors offer the model as an internally validated screening aid for high risk groups, pending outside testing.
plos-pone-0353853: He and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the age of the ancient city of Guge. Guge was a lost kingdom site in western Tibet, famed for its ruins and murals. The team combined carbon-14 dating of samples with old written records. Pinning down when key buildings rose helps historians place Guge in the wider story of Tibet and guards its past from guesswork.
plos-pone-0353953:
Zeng and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, present a better way to slim down point clouds, the millions of dots that scanners collect to map real scenes. Slimming cuts file size and computing load, but crude cuts either leave noise behind or erase sharp edges. Their method works at several scales at once.

Three ideas combine. A sliding filter smooths noise while guarding sharp features. Space is split into boxes guided by how much information each area holds, so dense areas keep detail and sparse areas waste less memory. A strengthened skeleton method then extracts the core shape of objects with fewer breaks. On their own scans of buildings, plants, and roads, and on a public test set, the method removed most noise. It kept edges well, and rebuilt surfaces with the lowest errors among the methods tried. The authors aim it at city modeling and scene rebuilding.
plos-pone-0354153:
Stefanie Michel and seven colleagues look for dormant herpes viruses waking up in intensive care patients with COVID-19, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from one German centre. They screened four hundred and fifty-five patients admitted between March 2020 and December 2021, testing blood and airway samples for two common herpes viruses that hide in the body for life.

Reactivation appeared in over a third of patients, typically within days of admission and more often the longer the stay. Herpes simplex reactivation marked a much rougher course: far lower survival, and more need for ventilators, artificial lung support, and dialysis. The authors cannot prove the virus caused the harm, but argue it flags the patients in deepest trouble.
plos-pone-0354353:
Eugene Tang and colleagues examine in 2026 ethnic gaps in care and outcomes six months after stroke across four regions of England. A national stroke audit supplied records, and a specialist review at six months is recommended for all survivors, though fewer than half receive one. The team compared attendance, later illness, and preventive treatment by ethnic group.

Attendance was similar overall, with Black and Asian patients slightly more likely to be reviewed after adjustment, often by phone. Yet both groups faced higher odds of another stroke or hospital return, and Black patients received less fat lowering treatment. Culturally fitting support is needed, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0354453:
Hoài Trần, K David Harrison, and colleagues describe how the Bahnar people of Vietnam's Central Highlands understand their forest through yang, the spirits or deities woven through daily life. Their 2026 ethnographic paper draws on extended fieldwork, tracing reciprocity between humans and spirits through house building, cooking, pathfinding, gong music, farming, and travel on rivers.

The spirit world is carried in the Bahnar language itself, in its vocabulary, sayings, songs, place names, and epics, passed on by people in many social roles. The authors argue this cosmology is the main lens through which the Bahnar perceive nature, guiding choices that incidentally conserve biodiversity. Their account positions Indigenous knowledge systems as working environmental philosophies, not folklore decoration.
plos-pone-0354753:
Nampetch Puengpong led a team of eight authors on this 2026 feeding trial with broiler chickens whose feed carried several fungal toxins at once. Mold toxins in grain quietly damage poultry health. More than four hundred chicks were split between clean feed, contaminated feed, and contaminated feed plus a blended detoxifier made of clays, yeast walls, and glucans.

Toxin-fed birds ate more yet converted feed worse early on, lost antibody strength, and showed fatty, inflamed livers. Adding the detoxifier restored much of the immune and liver picture. Puengpong presents it as practical protection for poultry farms.
plos-pone-0354953:
Yujie Cui and Lin Li analyse in 2026 how new digital forms of productivity might help China reach shared prosperity across its provinces. Panel data from thirty regions fed several methods that score overall progress, trace how the spread changes, and find which mixes of factors work together. Digital strength was split into foundation, industry, and development elements, all tied to talent.

Shared prosperity rose overall, with the east ahead of the west. Three winning mixes all paired digital elements with talent, and the path shifted over time from foundation toward fuller development. Regional gaps widened in two directions. The authors suggest tailored regional strategies to close them.
plos-pone-0355053:
Yiming Li, Hua Wang, and colleagues propose in 2026 a network for outlining embryo structures in images used during fertility treatment. Clear outlines help judge whether an embryo may implant, but embryos are see through, nested, and hard to label in bulk. Their single model has two heads: one paints the regions and one guides the overall shape using structure cues.

Two added modules sharpen hard, low contrast borders and gather features at several scales. On a public embryo dataset the method beat eleven rival semi supervised methods, and it also held up on a heart chamber dataset. Clearer outlines could support more consistent embryo grading.
plos-pone-0355253:
RETRACTED: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 retraction notice, withdrawing a study that had claimed a bamboo stem extract blocks tumour cell invasion and lung spread in lab models. Readers should not rely on that study's findings. Concerns centred on figures four through seven and on how the statistics were handled.

Several blot and cell panels appeared to overlap, some panels showed signs suggestive of splice lines, and one graph axis was mislabelled. The first author said original data were lost with age and could not rule out assembly errors. Methods named only one simple test, with no account of correction for many comparisons, leaving the results unresolved.
plos-pone-0355853:
Pritee Parwekar and colleagues built a deep learning method that ranks where calcium ions bind on proteins. Calcium binding sites steer signalling, enzyme control, and protein stability, so locating them matters. Their 2026 study focused on a calcium-binding protein from an amoeba parasite and ten changed versions of it.

Their ranking model reads protein features and orders predicted sites by binding strength. Its rankings tracked measured values closely across the variants. The study also compared the shapes calcium takes when held by different proteins, from simple cages to three-sided forms. Parwekar and colleagues argue the approach can guide later lab tests by pointing first to the most promising binding sites.
plos-pone-0355953:
Ali Forouhari and a Singapore-led team set out the plan for a five-year study of age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss, in Asian older adults. How the disease moves from early signs to late damage, and whom it strikes, varies across populations, and Asian data are thin. The cohort will recruit about fifteen hundred community adults aged fifty-five and over in Singapore and follow their eyes over time.

Regular imaging and checks will build one of the largest long-run records of this disease in Asia. Forouhari and colleagues aim to name the signs that best predict late disease, so screening programs can set referral thresholds on evidence rather than habit. The entry here is the study design paper, published ahead of results.
plos-pone-0356053:
Mahyar Abasi, Vahid Davatgaran, and Morteza Azizi address a safety problem on modern power lines in their 2026 PLOS ONE article. High voltage direct current lines increasingly carry power from wind farms, and when a fault strikes, operators must find it fast. Their protection algorithm works from measurements taken at one end of the line only, so it needs no communication link to the far end.

The scheme handles three jobs in one pass: spotting that a fault has occurred, deciding which pole and fault type are involved, and calculating where along the line it happened. It reads the brief surge patterns in current and voltage and builds the line's electrical coupling between poles into its location math. Tests in a standard simulation package checked the design under varied operating conditions.
plos-pone-0356253:
Nardos Gelana and colleagues interviewed thirty-nine health workers and program managers in Ethiopia's hardest-to-reach settings, urban slums and mobile pastoralist regions, about why routine childhood vaccination still misses children there. Their 2026 exploratory study, run in late 2023, used human-centered design and behavioral frameworks to structure the conversations and coded the answers thematically.

The obstacles were concrete: erratic vaccine supply, thin cold storage, low budgets, crushing workloads, and populations that move or crowd beyond official lists. What worked was equally concrete: genuine community engagement, local structures enlisted as partners, mobile teams, and private providers brought into the fold. Managers' top asks were supply chain repair and workforce support, both prerequisites for the creative outreach to matter.
plos-pone-0357053:
Erika Machtinger, Karen Poh, Laura Kenny, and Danielle Smarsh wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about ticks on horses. It is a participatory science study, enlisting horse owners and handlers as partners. The work covers identifying ticks, monitoring them, and physical barriers meant to reduce bites.

Barriers to entry run through the study: what stops people from joining the science, and what physical barriers stop ticks from reaching horses. Tick bites spread diseases to horses and riders, so practical prevention matters on farms. Equine veterinarians and extension workers can use findings about what owners will actually do, not just what works in a lab.
plos-pone-0357153: Predicting ultra-high-performance concrete’s compressive strength saves costly lab testing. This paper compared machine learning models for the task head-to-head. The bake-off identifies which algorithms engineers can actually trust with their mix designs.
plos-pone-0357753:
Joan K Monin and four colleagues ask how many American family caregivers lean on AI chatbots, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Caregivers of people with chronic and worsening conditions are stretched thin, and formal support is scarce. The team used a national survey wave of thirteen hundred caregivers, collected in late summer and autumn 2025, mixing structured questions with written answers they coded for themes.

About a third of respondents used chatbots at all, and a quarter of those users turned to them for caregiving help, from information to emotional support. Personality played a role: people higher in openness were more likely to use a chatbot for care tasks. The study also weighed internet skill, thinking ability, stress, and the care relationship. The snapshot shows a support tool quietly entering family care before services have caught up.
plos-pone-0358253:
Yamei Zhang and Xiaohu Liu build a neural network to hear failing bearings before they seize, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rolling bearings support nearly every rotating machine, and their faults hide under noise and shifting speeds. Their network reads vibration signals at several scales at once. Then it applies two kinds of attention. One reweights which signal channels matter. The other spotlights the brief fault impulses in the stream. Only then does it classify the fault type.

On the standard public bearing dataset, the system reached accuracy above ninety-nine percent in the hardest cross condition tests, where the machine's speed and load change between training and testing. Under heavy added noise it still held above ninety-two percent. It beat three recent rival methods on accuracy and related scores while running cheaper and faster. For factory maintenance teams, that combination promises earlier warnings from the sensors they already own.
plos-pone-0358353:
Juan-José Gallego led a team of eight authors testing eye movement checks in liver patients, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cirrhosis can cloud the brain in a subtle condition called minimal hepatic encephalopathy. The standard psychometric score misses some early cases. The team asked whether tracking eye movements catches changes the score labels as absent.

Gallego's study found that eye movement analysis does detect early neurological changes in those patients. Eyes are easy to test, cheap, and hard to fake or practice, unlike paper tests. Earlier detection lets doctors adjust treatment and warn about driving safety sooner. The work offers clinics a practical add-on test for a complication that quietly affects daily life.
plos-pone-0358453:
Ming Fei Li, Lavania Nagendran, Christopher Kiru, Lauren Schroeder, and David Samson published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It asks a playful question with real science behind it: who is disrupting whom at night, humans or their dogs? The authors examine nighttime activity patterns of both.

People often blame dogs for broken sleep, but human schedules may disturb dogs just as much. Recording activity for both sides of the bed gives an even-handed picture of shared nights. Sleep researchers and pet behavior specialists can use this two-way view to advise households where restless nights are blamed on the dog by default.
plos-pone-0358553: Sharafi and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on bull sperm and water movement across cell walls. They measured how well sperm handle water that is too strong or too weak in salts. Age, breed, and which collection round the sperm came from all played a role. The findings matter for freezing sperm, since ice damage depends on how water leaves and enters cells.
plos-pone-0358753:
Tingting Zhu and Yuhuan Wang study how live streamed shopping affects young buyers' loyalty to old, heritage brands, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Brands with long histories carry craft traditions but must win over shoppers who buy through video streams. The authors asked which parts of a live session actually build that bond, focusing on excitement and the feeling of a real relationship with the brand.

They surveyed just over four hundred consumers aged eighteen to forty who had watched heritage brand streams. Both chatting with the host and engaging with products raised viewers' sense of social presence and belief that the brand was genuine. Those feelings fed emotional excitement, which in turn strengthened identification with the brand. The chain gives heritage sellers a practical map for designing streams that younger audiences trust.
plos-pone-0358953:
Xu Li and Yufeng Qiao use public gene data to hunt for shared markers between two rare autoimmune diseases, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. One condition inflames and scars the kidneys under attack from the immune system's own antibodies. The other swells glands and organs with immune cells. Case reports hint the two overlap, but nobody had compared their gene activity across tissues.

Working from a kidney dataset for the first disease and a salivary gland dataset for the second, they screened hundreds of altered genes and used machine learning to narrow the field. Two genes, ITGAM and CXCL1, emerged as candidate markers common to both, and immune pathways dominated the shared signal. The authors frame the pair as leads for diagnosis research, noting the small samples behind the second dataset.
plos-pone-0359153:
Hongyi Yuan and four colleagues present a software method, published in PLOS ONE in 2026, for sorting huge collections of single cells by their gene activity. Modern sequencing can profile hundreds of thousands of cells at once, but grouping those cells into types gets slow and unreliable at that scale. Their framework, called scLTF, is built to handle the volume.

The method first makes rough groups with a fast graph based algorithm, then picks the most typical cells from each group. A transformer model, the kind of network behind modern language tools, then refines the groups step by step. On several real datasets it matched or beat leading deep learning methods on accuracy while using only a fraction of their running time.
plos-pone-0359353: Ju and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on forecasting how long freeway incidents last. Crashes and breakdowns tie up traffic, and crews must guess when lanes will clear. The team applied machine learning to predict incident duration. Sharper guesses help traffic centers warn drivers, set detours, and send the right crews to the scene.
plos-pone-0359553: de Goede and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a new interview for moral injury in soldiers. Moral injury is the lasting pain from acts that clash with a person's values. The team built a military version of a clinical interview and tested whether it can be used in practice. A workable interview is a first step toward care for a wound that standard trauma checks may miss.
plos-pone-0359653:
Vaishaali Gunalan and co-authors set out a study protocol in 2026 for testing whether color vision checks can catch early diabetic retinopathy. This eye disease, a complication of diabetes, damages the retina and is a leading cause of blindness in working age adults. It usually causes no symptoms until the damage is advanced, so screening decides who keeps their sight.

Their project, shortened to CODER, proposes color vision assessment as the screening tool, since color perception can falter early in the disease. A protocol paper fixes the design, measures, and analysis plan before results exist, keeping the eventual findings honest. A cheap, quick test that community clinics could run would widen screening far beyond specialist eye centers.
plos-pone-0359853:
Yi Zhang, Li Zhang, Jihui Hu, Meng Zhang, and Xiapei Peng published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study of stroke survivors in middle and older age. The authors examine pre-stroke social participation, how active a person was socially before the stroke, and its association with current physical resilience.

The comparison runs across frailty levels, from robust survivors to very frail ones. Physical resilience is the body's ability to bounce back after stress, and it may rest partly on a person's earlier social life. Rehabilitation teams planning recovery support are the readers who could use social history this way.
pmc-13233853:
Fawzi, Asker, and Yousef test how deep concrete beams stand up to twisting. Their beams use high-strength concrete and cross-inclined stirrups, the steel ties set at a slant inside the beam. Nine beams were built and loaded under pure torsion, a twisting force that deep beams in bridges and buildings must sometimes carry.

The team measured strength and how much each beam deformed before failing. Slanted ties may grip twisting cracks better than straight ones, but proof needs tests, not theory. Their results give designers the grounding for safer and cheaper deep beams, where guessing at torsion strength risks either waste or failure.

All states were called on to respect the deal. They should help put its pledges into practice. The Secretary-General had to report on its use in his regular reports. The signers would supply facts for those reports. The deal aimed to calm a region long troubled by meddling across borders.
un-sc-res-1553:
UNIFIL, the force in southern Lebanon, was renewed in the summer of 2004. On 29 July 2004 the Security Council extended its mandate until 31 January 2005. The Secretary-General had recommended exactly that term. His report noted that Israel had completed its 2000 withdrawal. Lebanon was slowly sending its own army south. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and borders in strong terms.

Lebanon had to keep extending its authority across the south. Deploying its armed forces there was central to that task. The Council also repeated the terms set when the force was created in 1978. All parties had to cooperate with UNIFIL in full. The renewal was routine, but the border stayed armed and tense.
un-sc-res-1653: Security Council Resolution 1653 survives in this collection as a transcription of the United Nations official record. The heading number is its permanent address in the sequence, the form by which officials cite it. Inside that address sits a complete decision: stated grounds first, then the operative clauses through which the Council acts.
un-sc-res-1753:
Liberia's diamond sanctions were lifted by the Security Council on 27 April 2007. Liberia had worked with the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme to control its rough diamond trade. Its government had sent the committee a detailed certificate of origin plan on 4 April. The Panel of Experts had reported on the progress made toward the conditions set in resolution 1521 (2003).

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminated the diamond measures imposed by resolution 1521 (2003) and renewed in 2006. It judged that enough progress had been made toward meeting the stated conditions. The Kimberley Process was asked to report within ninety days on Liberia's application to join the scheme. Liberia was called to carry out the expert mission's advice for the period after admission. The Council would review the lifting once it had the experts' final report, due by 6 June 2007, and the Kimberley report.
un-sc-res-1853: From 2008, Resolution 1853 adds a Council decision to this run of record texts, kept through a copy made by English Wikisource. The act is built in the usual way: first the shared facts, then the steps the members chose. For readers who want to check what the Council truly ordered, that full build is what counts, and it is kept here whole.
un-sc-res-253: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 253, catalogued here at 1966. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-353:
Cyprus came under formal Council review in Resolution 353, adopted unanimously on 20 July 1974. A coup backed from Athens had toppled the island's government five days earlier. Turkish troops landed that morning. Fighting and bloodshed spread across the island, and the whole eastern Mediterranean felt explosive.

The Council calls on all states to respect Cyprus's sovereignty and unity of territory. Every party must cease fire at once as a first step. Foreign military action against the island must end without delay. Troops present outside treaty rights must pull out. Greece, Turkey, and the United Kingdom are told to open talks at once. The aim is peace and a return to lawful government.
un-sc-res-453: The Council considered Saint Lucia in Resolution 453, adopted unanimously on 12 September 1979. The Caribbean island had applied to join the United Nations. The Council studied the application as the Charter requires. It then gave its answer in a single line. The Council recommends to the General Assembly that Saint Lucia be admitted as a member. Such votes are the gate every new state must pass. The Assembly acted on the advice days later, and the island took its seat.
un-sc-res-53: The matter of Palestine was settled in Resolution 53, adopted on 7 July 1948 by eight votes to none, with three abstentions. A first truce in the fighting was about to run out. The UN mediator on the ground had wired the Council on 5 July. The Council sends an urgent appeal to the parties. It asks them to accept in principle a longer truce. The length would be set in talks with the mediator. The text is a single sentence, sent to buy time for peace work.
un-sc-res-853:
Armenia and Azerbaijan are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 853, adopted on 29 July 1993. Fighting over Nagorno-Karabakh had grown worse. The district of Agdam in Azerbaijan had just been seized. Large numbers of civilians had fled, and a grave relief emergency was building in the region.

The Council condemns the seizure of Agdam and all other land taken in recent fighting. It demands an end to the fighting at once. The occupying forces must pull out fully and without conditions. The text backs the Minsk Group's peace work and urges Armenia to press the Karabakh Armenians to comply. States should stop sending weapons that could feed the conflict.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1253, adopted on 28 July 1999, is the Security Council's short response to a membership application. Having examined the request from the Kingdom of Tonga, a Pacific island kingdom, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that Tonga be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That recommendation is the step the UN Charter requires before the Assembly can vote a new member in.

Countries that supply troops to peacekeeping missions carry the risk on the ground, yet they had little say when mandates were written. That imbalance is the subject of this text of 13 June 2001. It follows a Council debate held that January on giving troop contributors a stronger voice.

New ways of consulting those countries before and during missions are set out, including private meetings and regular reports on the talks. The Council promised to weigh their views when deciding on peacekeeping operations. It also backed better planning support, including joint mission teams, and asked its peacekeeping working group to keep improving how the United Nations runs operations.

Just before Christmas 2002, Kabul hosted a rare show of regional goodwill. The Afghan cabinet signed a pact with six neighbors. The six were China, Iran, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. All pledged to live as good neighbors. None would meddle in Afghan affairs. Resolution 1453, passed on 24 December 2002, cheered the deal.

The Council backed the Kabul pact in full. It called on all states to keep its terms. The Secretary-General had to track how well the pact held. His notes would form part of his routine reports on the country. The deal fit the Bonn plan, the road map for rebuilding the Afghan state after the Taliban fell.

Gabon became independent from France on 17 August 1960. Its application for UN membership reached New York within days. Resolution 153 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The decision came at the packed 891st meeting. That single session recommended several African states for admission.

The Council advised the General Assembly to admit the Gabon Republic. The Assembly did so in September. Gabon's oil wealth was still mostly undiscovered or untapped. Politically, the country joined the francophone African group at the UN. The resolution is one line long. Behind it stood the rapid unwinding of France's African empire during the summer of 1960.

South Lebanon, not the Golan Heights, is the stage here. The force there, UNIFIL, had stood since 1978. Beirut asked on 9 July 2004 for six more months of the watch. The chief's report of 21 July warned of strain along the border. Resolution 1553 passed with no dissent on 29 July 2004.

UNIFIL's term now ran to 31 January 2005. The Council backed Lebanon's claim to its full land. It urged Beirut to send its own troops south in force. Both sides had to let UN patrols move freely. Breaches of the Blue Line, by sea, land, and air, drew sharp blame. Mine clearing by the force won praise, as did gifts of mine maps.

Peace and security in Africa's Great Lakes region are taken up in a wide statement of 27 January 2006. The region had suffered a decade of wars, and the 1994 genocide in Rwanda is recalled with condemnation. Growing cooperation among the region's states, the African Union, and the United Nations is welcomed.

Great Lakes countries are urged to deepen their cooperation, agree confidence-building measures, and respect each other's borders and independence. Those guilty of grave crimes in the region are to be brought to justice, with an end to impunity. The world community, aid groups, and donors are also asked to support the region's recovery. That support covers disarmament efforts and the return of refugees, so the recent peace deals in Congo and Burundi will hold.

Resolution 1753, adopted on 27 April 2007, lifts the ban on Liberian diamonds. The embargo had been imposed in 2003, when rough diamonds helped fund Liberia's war. Since then Liberia had joined the Kimberley Process, the certification scheme designed to keep conflict diamonds off world markets, and had proposed a certificate-of-origin system that UN experts reviewed in April.

Having judged that enough progress had been made, and acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminated the diamond measures first set in resolution 1521. It encouraged the Kimberley Process to report back within ninety days on how Liberia was doing. For a country rebuilding under President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, legal diamond exports meant revenue the war economy had stolen.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is extended once more on 19 December 2008. The text again spells out the embargo's exemptions for the African Union mission and for help building up Somalia's own security forces. A separate resolution the month before had added targeted sanctions on people blocking peace in Somalia.

The group's mandate is extended so it can keep investigating violations and reporting through the sanctions committee. The committee is asked to act on the group's findings, including by visiting the region and pressing states to enforce the rules. The renewal kept the monitors in place as the interim government's hold weakened and the insurgency around Mogadishu grew.

Cyprus peace talks set the scene for Resolution 1953, adopted on 14 December 2010. Full negotiations had made progress since 2008, but the pace had slowed and the status quo was called unsustainable. A Limnitis crossing point had opened in October 2010. Demining was advancing, and the Committee on Missing Persons kept working.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 June 2011. It calls on the two leaders to speed up the talks and draw up a practical plan to settle the main disagreements before a January 2011 meeting with the Secretary-General. It urges public messaging focused on common ground and more civil-society involvement. It again asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. A report, including settlement contingency planning, is due by 1 June 2011.

Sanctions on Southern Rhodesia became much wider on 29 May 1968, when the Council adopted Resolution 253 unanimously. Earlier and narrower measures had failed to end the white minority rebellion. The illegal regime had also carried out fresh executions, which brought sharp condemnation.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council ordered all member states to cut off nearly all trade with Rhodesia. Funds and investment had to be blocked. Airlines had to stop flying there, and emigration to the colony was to be prevented. The Council condemned political repression in Rhodesia. Arrests, detentions, trials, and executions were all named. Britain, as the ruling power, was again pressed to end the rebellion and let the people of Rhodesia win their rights.

Turkish troops landed in Cyprus on 20 July 1974, days after a coup backed by Greece. That same day the Council adopted Resolution 353 unanimously. Cyprus's president, Archbishop Makarios, had already asked for foreign forces to leave. The members called the violence a grave threat to peace in the eastern Mediterranean.

Every side was told to stop firing at once. The Council demanded an end to foreign military intervention. Soldiers present without treaty rights had to withdraw without delay. Greece, Turkey, and Britain were urged to negotiate quickly. Talks would aim to restore peace and constitutional rule. The UN peacekeeping force in Cyprus won full backing.

Saint Lucia, a small Caribbean island, became independent from Britain in February 1979. Admission to the United Nations was a natural next step. Its application reached New York as document S/13530. Resolution 453 was adopted unanimously on 12 September 1979. The Council examined the bid at its 2167th meeting.

Members recommended that Saint Lucia be admitted. The General Assembly followed the advice that same month. For a microstate, a UN seat carries real weight. It brings a vote equal to any large power's. It also opens doors to aid agencies and treaties. Saint Lucia's smooth admission shows the routine, welcoming side of the Council's work.

A fragile truce paused the first Arab-Israeli war in the summer of 1948. The UN Mediator worked to stretch that pause. His telegram of 5 July 1948 reached the Council with an urgent request. Resolution 53 followed on 7 July 1948. Eight members voted yes. Syria, the Ukrainian republic, and the Soviet Union abstained.

The whole text is one appeal. Interested parties were urged to accept, in principle, a longer truce. The length would be settled in talks with the Mediator. The resolution is tiny, yet it shows the Council learning peacekeeping by improvisation. Every extra week of truce was meant to save lives and keep diplomacy alive.

Croatia had declared independence as Yugoslavia fell apart. War was already burning across the young republic. Still, its government applied to join the United Nations. Resolution 753, adopted without a vote on 18 May 1992, handled that application. The Council examined the request at its 3076th meeting.

The answer was a recommendation. Members advised the General Assembly to admit the Republic of Croatia. Under the Charter, the Assembly makes the final call on new members. It did so days later. Croatia's admission gave its independence a firm legal footing. It also signaled that Yugoslavia's breakup was being accepted, state by state, in New York.

The seizure of Agdam escalates the Nagorno-Karabakh war in Resolution 853, adopted on 29 July 1993. Relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan had worsened further since Resolution 822 in April. The parties had accepted a timetable of urgent steps, but fighting grew and the district of Agdam in Azerbaijan was taken. Large numbers of civilians were displaced.

The Council condemns the seizure of Agdam and all other recently occupied areas of Azerbaijan, and condemns attacks on civilians and shelling of inhabited areas. It demands an immediate end to hostilities and the complete, unconditional withdrawal of the occupying forces from Agdam and the other areas. It urges Armenia's government to press the Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh to comply, and urges all states to supply no weapons or munitions that could deepen the conflict. It backs the CSCE Minsk Group's peace efforts and its planned monitor mission, and calls for unimpeded relief access.
whewell-plurality-worlds-1853:
William Whewell was a master of many fields at Cambridge. In 1853 he put out a bold tract with no name on it. The tract argues that Earth may stand alone as a home of life. It struck at the claim of a host of lived-in worlds.

Whewell weighs heat, light, and the size of each planet. He holds that most worlds are too hot, too cold, or too wild for life. The tract drew a sharp reply from David Brewster. The clash set off ten years of print debate on the worlds.
william-newburgh-history-stevenson-1853:
William of Newburgh, an Augustinian canon in Yorkshire, wrote his History of English Affairs in the 1190s. It covers the years from the Norman Conquest to 1198. Joseph Stevenson translated the work in 1853. William is often called the most critical of the English historians of the twelfth century, and he earns the praise.

He weighs his sources, mocks Geoffrey of Monmouth's tales of Arthur as lies, and tells even wonders with a raised brow. The reigns of Stephen, Henry II, and Richard pass under his cool judgment. His tale of the civil war of Stephen's time is a chief source for the anarchy. Northern voices are rare in this age, and his is the best.
zoist-vol-11-1853:
Volume eleven of The Zoist spans April 1853 to January 1854. Elliotson edits on, his journal of cerebral physiology and mesmerism in its eleventh year. Case reports of trance cures and painless procedures keep arriving. The somnambulist reports now share an age with table turning and spirit circles.

Mesmerists in these pages claim prior right to the new wonders. Critics answer that trance and fraud explain them all. The thirteen volumes of the run form the movement's archive entire. Volume eleven belongs to its final stretch. The writing stays earnest, detailed, and combative by turns. It records a world of practice that official journals scorned.
